entry.title: The Unsung Hero of SAP GRC Access Control: Understanding Action Usage Synch
entry.content:
Every SAP GRC Access Control administrator has probably heard the phrases "transactional log" or "action usage data" thrown around in discussions. But how many people have actually stopped to think about where that data comes from, what makes it reliable, and what happens when the plumbing behind it quietly breaks? This post pulls back the curtain on the Action Usage Synch report — the background report that keeps GRC's action usage picture accurate — and explains why misconfiguring a single parameter can silently poison your compliance data for months.
 
What Is Action Usage Sync, and Who Uses the Data?
 
At its heart, Action Usage Synch (GRAC_ACTION_USAGE_SYNC) is a background report that bridges two worlds: the raw transaction logs living on your connected SAP systems (plugin systems), and the neatly structured GRC database tables that power reports, dashboards, and risk analysis. Every time a user executes a transaction code, initiates a WebDynpro application, consumes an OData service, or opens a Fiori Tile on a managed system, that execution is recorded in the system's performance statistics (STAD — System Transaction Analysis and Diagnosis), Gateway log, or Frontend statistics (FESR — FrontEnd Statistics Records). The Action Usage Sync job harvests those logs and translates them into two GRC-owned tables: 'GRACACTUSAGE', which stores individual execution events with full timestamps, user IDs, connectors, terminal info, and transaction codes; and 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE', which maintains a rolled-up management view showing the execution count and last execution date per user-action-connector combination.
 
The consumers of this data are broader than most people realise. Role-level usage analysis in GRC Access Control relies on it — when you run a role usage report and see that a role's critical actions were "last used 14 months ago," that number comes from 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE'. Risk owners who want to know whether a SoD-violating action combination was actually exercised, or just theoretically possible, look here. The Emergency Access Management module also has its own flavour of this mechanism: when a Firefighter User logs in via a Firefighter ID, the exact same GRACACTUSAGE data is eventually consolidated to the particular Firefighter Session by matching the timestamps. The connection between the Firefighter Session and the Action Usage data is stored in the 'GRACFFREPMAPP' table.
 
How It Works: A Journey Across Two Systems
 
The report runs on the GRC central system, but the actual transaction logs it needs are sitting on the connected managed (plugin) systems. This cross-system reach is what makes the architecture interesting.
 
When the job starts, it first resolves which connectors to process. It translates the user-provided connector range into a proper list of active connectors. Next, it determines the timestamp for each connector from which the sync should start. This information is stored in the 'GRACTASKEXECSTMP' table — a small but critical bookkeeping table that records the last successful execution timestamp per task per connector. The task key for this is 'ACTION_USAGE_SYNC'. This timestamp becomes the 'FROM' timestamp for the next run's log query, ensuring the job is always incremental and only asks for data that is genuinely new.
 
The actual data retrieval is where the RFC call happens. For SAP ABAP connectors — the typical case — the code resolves the RFC destination from the connector configuration, then calls a dedicated function module on the target system. This function module lives on the plugin component (GRCPINW, GRCPIBAS) and is responsible for reading STAD and — if enabled — OData Gateway and FESR logs there. The results — user name, transaction code, timestamp, terminal, program name, and a transaction ID — travel back to the main GRC system over RFC, which receives the data and maps it into the internal action log structure.
 
Back on the main GRC system, the report processes the returned records in batches. The 'Time Period' parameter (defaulting to 3,600 seconds, i.e. one hour) controls the size of each time slice sent to the RFC call. The total time range from the last execution timestamp to now is divided into chunks of that many seconds, and the RFC is called once per chunk. This prevents a single call from pulling an enormous payload after a long gap, and it also allows intermediate progress to be committed to the database between chunks. After processing each batch, the code persists individual records to 'GRACACTUSAGE' and upserts the aggregated execution counts in 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE'. Alert action logs are also updated.
 
One deduplication mechanism deserves special mention: the 'GRACACTTRANS' table. This table stores connector–user ID–action–program ID–transaction ID tuples for recently seen transaction executions. Before inserting a new record from the RFC response, the code checks whether that particular action and program combination for the particular user has already been processed for the particular transaction. If it has, the record is skipped. After each successful run, 'GRACACTTRANS' is cleaned up: records older than the Retention Period in seconds (defaulting to 432,000 seconds — five days) are deleted. This sliding cleanup window is there purely to cap the table's growth while still protecting against duplicates across consecutive runs. The duplicate check is essential due to how STAD information is transformed into Action Usage information in GRC. Without this check, execution counts would not be accurate and the size of 'GRACACTUSAGE' would grow exponentially.
 
Parameters and Scheduling Frequency: Why Every Second Counts
 
The report exposes four parameters on its selection screen:
 
Connector: Restricts which connectors are processed. Leaving it empty processes all configured connectors. In large landscapes with many connectors, scoping this per connector and running parallel jobs staggered slightly in time can significantly improve throughput.
 
User: Restricts data collection for Firefighter Action Usage Synch to a specific set of users. This is relevant only in special cases when SAP Support instructs you to do so; for normal execution the value should always be completely empty.
 
Time Period: This is the parameter that most frequently causes operational grief. It defines the size of each RFC call's time slice in seconds. The default is 3,600 seconds (one hour), which serves a good balance between execution time and resource requirements. Decreasing the value means fewer resources are required (time and memory) to collect the action data per call; however, more RFC roundtrips will be required, and the overall execution time of the job will increase due to RFC overhead. Increasing the value means faster execution of the sync job, but significantly more resources will be required to collect the action data per call.
 
Retention Period: This parameter controls the retention period of the 'GRACACTTRANS' deduplication table, defaulting to 432,000 seconds (five days). Any data older than the configured time in seconds will be removed from 'GRACACTTRANS', and the duplicate check will no longer be able to detect it as a duplicate.
 
For the scheduling frequency, the answer depends on how current you need your action usage data to be. The standard recommendation is to run the job every hour. This ensures that the job collects all data created in the last hour, providing up-to-date information in your main GRC system. It also gives enough time to ensure that the action data is properly collected.
 
Running the job less frequently — say, daily — is not inherently wrong, but you will encounter longer execution times and you increase the risk of missing action information if you fail to detect that the job is not running properly. Because STAD data is stored for only 48 hours in the default configuration (for more information, check the profile parameter 'stat/max_files'), if you fail to collect the data within this timeframe, that data will be lost and can never be collected again.
 
Common Issue #1 — The User Field Is Filled When It Shouldn't Be
 
This one causes more confusion than you'd expect. When the Users parameter is populated, the report takes a completely different code path. Instead of collecting the normal action usage information, it executes a special process designed to collect data for Firefighter usage in emergency cases only. This is intentional design: populating the user field signals "I am syncing a specific Firefighter session," and GRC switches to the SPM connector infrastructure accordingly. In normal circumstances this is never required — this process is handled by the Firefighter Sync job — so you should only use it if specifically instructed to do so (mostly in cases where Action Usage Sync has never been executed because your business does not require that information, yet the Firefighter Log Sync job is not working for some reason).
 
The practical problem arises when an administrator — trying to narrow down a test run or debug a single user's data — enters a regular business user in the user field of the general Action Usage Sync job. The job will attempt to use the SPM connector path for a non-SPM user on a connector that may not have SPM configured at all. The run will collect information, but it will not register it in the Alert table and will not update the general Action Usage timestamp. The data collected in this mode is simply not regular Action Usage data, so you will not get accurate action-related information and metrics, and the root cause will not be immediately obvious.
 
The rule is simple: to run general Action Usage Synch, the user field should always be completely empty. Not even a whitespace or any wildcard character (* or ?) should be entered in this field. User-scoped runs are intended for emergency cases only and should be performed only when instructed by an expert.
 
Common Issue #2 — The Time Period Parameter Is Set Too Low or Too High
 
Too low: If Time Period is set to, say, 30 seconds, the report will issue 120 RFC calls to cover a single hour of data. This is technically functional but will hammer both the GRC system and the target system with rapid-fire RFC connections. Under heavy connector loads with many connectors, this can cause RFC work process saturation on the target. Worse, if each call takes more than a second or two due to STAD read overhead, the processing time for a single connector can stretch to minutes — blowing through the available batch window. This could increase the time required to finish the job, which could lead to consecutive scheduling issues. The safe lower bound is around 60 seconds (one minute) for systems with moderate usage volumes; however, if you need to set the value that low, it could indicate an improper resource configuration on your backend system. The optimal lower bound is 150–300 seconds.
 
Too high: The opposite extreme is setting the Time Period to a very large value — for instance, 86,400 seconds (one full day) — to "simplify" the chunking. The problem here is that a single RFC call now requests a full day's worth of STAD data in one go. STAD is not a small log source on busy production systems. Very large STAD reads can time out at the RFC layer, return with a communication failure, and leave the job's watermark timestamp un-updated. The next run will then attempt the same oversized time window again, fail again, and the data gap grows. If you observe frequent TSV_TNEW_PAGE_ALLOC_FAILED or TIME_OUT dumps in your connected backend system, that is a pretty good indication that the value is too high and you need to decrease it. This can occur even with the default value. In that case you should decrease the value and find the highest value at which dumps are no longer observed. STAD has an optimal read window of around 10 minutes, so setting the value somewhere between 300 and 600 seconds should work well in most cases.
 
Common Issue #3 — The Job Was Never Run, or Has Been Silent for a Long Time
 
This is the scenario that GRC teams tend to discover late — typically during an audit or a risk analysis review, when someone notices that action usage data for a critical system is either missing entirely or frozen at a date from twelve months ago.
 
When the 'GRACTASKEXECSTMP' entry for a connector does not exist (the job has never run), the report treats the start timestamp as empty, which the downstream code interprets as "start from the beginning of available data" — translated to the beginning of the UNIX epoch (19700101000000). In practice, this means the RFC call on the target system will attempt to retrieve the entire available STAD history — potentially weeks or months of transaction data — in chunks of the Time Period value each. This is the operational equivalent of asking someone to retype a library by hand. Even with an optimal Time Period value, an initial sync covering all data on an active system can take hours of continuous runtime and thousands of RFC calls. During this time the job holds RFC work processes on both systems and generates significant load. And — based on STAD retention — it will only actually find meaningful action data for the last 48 hours.
 
A similarly problematic situation arises when the job has been running but then stopped for an extended period — perhaps because the scheduled job variant was accidentally deleted, or the system connector was temporarily deactivated and then forgotten.
 
How to resolve it: There is a fully compliant but slow way, and there is a faster, more efficient option whose compliance depends on your policy.
 
The fully compliant way is to stop the currently scheduled Action Usage Synch (if it is running) and start it in ad-hoc mode with properly set parameters. Run the job until it finishes on its own, then restart it again in ad-hoc mode. Repeat this process until the job finishes within the required scheduling frequency, at which point you will be able to schedule it. The first few executions might take hours or even days depending on how long ago the last successful execution was, and the job will probably only collect data from the last 48 hours (or whatever the STAD retention value is set to on the backend system). Each iteration should complete more and more quickly, and eventually the job will finish within the desired scheduling window (SAP's recommendation is hourly execution). Using this method, you collect all available data and the job sets the appropriate timestamps and values (execution counts, last execution timestamps, etc.) as if it had been running throughout.
 
The faster option is to use the report GRAC_EAM_TASK_TIMESTAMP_UPDATE to set the last successful execution timestamp of the Action Usage Sync manually. Before doing this, first consult your compliance coordinator to confirm that this approach is acceptable under your policy. If it is, run the report in SA38/SE38, set the connector, enter the desired timestamp in the format YYYYMMDDHHMISS (for example, 13:45:00 on 26 April 2019 would be entered as 20190426134500), select "Action Usage Synch (All User)", and execute. This will set the timestamp in the 'GRACTASKEXECSTMP' table, after which you can run the job in the same ad-hoc manner described above — but it will complete significantly faster since it will not start from "the beginning."
 
For both the never-run case and the stale case, always check the GRC application log after the first successful run. Navigate to the log and filter by category 'ACT_SYNC' or program 'GRAC_ACTION_USAGE_SYNC', and verify that the run completed without RFC errors or return code failures. A successful run will log a confirming completion message for each connector. Any 'E'-type messages pointing to `Plugin connection returned with error` or `Connector not found` indicate that the connector infrastructure itself needs attention before the data sync can succeed.
 
Common Issue #4 — Missing Authorization Causes Missing Usernames
 
This is also a common issue that is frequently found and poses a significant problem: it cannot be repaired, and if you do not detect it early, your data can be corrupted for a long time. The sync job runs hourly, the Time Period parameter is set optimally, the job runs flawlessly and without errors — yet you do not see any action-related information in any GRC reports or screens. You see that the 'GRACACTUSAGE' and 'GRACMGMTACTUSAGE' tables are populated with data. Seemingly no error, no issue... so what went wrong? If you look at the 'GRACACTUSAGE' table closely, you can see one small clue. The User IDs look odd — as if someone replaced all the actual usernames with random gibberish characters. This is not a coincidence or a bug; it is a privacy configuration of STAD. STAD will conceal User IDs unless the user attempting to retrieve them — in our case the RFC connection user configured in SM59 for the configured connector — has the authorization object S_TOOLS_EX with the value S_TOOLS_EX_A for the AUTH field. This authorization is most likely missing from the RFC user on your connected backend system, which is why it cannot read the User IDs.
 
Common Issue #5 — Time Is of the Essence
 
The last common issue is incorrect timezone or timezone rule configuration across your backend system's OS, database, and SAP system configuration. All three must be configured to use the same timezone and the same timezone rule. This ensures that each system calculates the requested timestamps correctly. If any of them is misconfigured, data may not be read accurately and may not be returned to GRC correctly. To detect any misconfiguration, you can run report 'RSDBTIME' on both your main GRC system and your connected backend system. This can reveal any major misconfiguration. Correcting the values should resolve missing or improperly collected logs.
 
Closing Thoughts
 
Action Usage Synch is one of those jobs that is easy to underestimate because it does its work quietly in the background. When it runs correctly, it is invisible. When it breaks — wrong user filter, wrong time slice, wrong timezone, long-dormant watermark, missing authorization — the failure tends to be silent too: no alarms, no obvious dashboard warnings, just slowly staling compliance data waiting to embarrass you at the next audit cycle. Moreover, the data cannot be repaired; you will only have accurate data from the point at which you resolved the root cause.
 
Taking five minutes to understand its parameters, scheduling it at a sane frequency, and periodically verifying its application logs is a small investment for a large return. The data it produces powers some of GRC's most valuable risk reduction capabilities. Treat the scheduler like the compliance instrument it is.

entry.title: Automating SAP SD Material Pricing Using a Rolling 5-Day Market Price Average
entry.content:
Introduction

In SAP Sales and Distribution (SD), the base price of a material is commonly determined using condition type PR00 in the pricing procedure. In some businesses, material prices fluctuate daily based on market rates published by external pricing portals.

Maintaining these prices manually can be time-consuming and may result in outdated prices being used during sales order creation.

In this blog, I will explain how to automate the PR00 base price calculation in SAP SD using daily high and low market prices, a custom table that retains five days of price history, and a custom pricing routine.

1. Business Requirement

The business requirement was to calculate the material's base price automatically using market data received from an external portal. The solution needed to meet the following requirements:

  • Fetch the daily high and low prices for relevant products from an external market data source.
  • Store the retrieved prices in SAP on a daily basis using a background job.
  • Retain only the latest five available days of price history for each product.
  • Calculate the average price based on the daily high and low values.
  • Automatically populate condition type PR00 during sales order pricing.
  • Allow users to manually override the calculated price when required.

The objective was to reduce manual price maintenance and ensure that the sales order uses a price derived from recent market data.

2. Solution Overview

The solution consists of two main processes.

Process 1: Daily Market Price Update

A custom ABAP program retrieves the market prices from the external portal and updates a custom SAP table. A background job executes this program periodically. The table retains five days of price history, while older records are removed automatically.

Process 2: Sales Order Price Determination

When a user creates a sales order and enters a material, SAP determines the applicable market product code, reads the five-day price history, calculates the average, and returns the result to PR00 through a custom alternative calculation routine.

3. Calculating the Daily Market Price

The external portal provides the highest and lowest prices for a product for each available pricing date.

The daily midpoint is calculated as follows:

Daily Mid Price = (Daily High Price + Daily Low Price) / 2

For example, consider the following market data for a product.

Day High PriceLow PriceMid Price
Day 1120100110
Day 2130110120
Day 3125105115
Day 4140120130
Day 5135115125

The five-day average is calculated using the daily midpoint for each of the five days.

Five-Day Average = Sum of the five daily midpoints / 5

Using the example above:

Five-Day Average = (110 + 120 + 115 + 130 + 125) / 5

Calculated Base Price = 120

This value becomes the proposed base price for the material, subject to the applicable pricing logic.

4. Storing Market Prices in SAP

A custom ABAP program retrieves the high and low market prices from the external source and stores them in a custom SAP table.

The relevant information includes:

  • Product Code: Identifies the product in the external market data feed.
  • Price Date: Identifies the date associated with the market price.
  • High Price: The highest published price for that date.
  • Low Price: The lowest published price for that date.

A scheduled background job runs the program to refresh the market data. The custom table retains the latest five available days of history for each product, and older records are deleted automatically.

This approach keeps the data required for price calculation readily available in SAP without maintaining an unlimited history in the operational table.

5. Mapping SAP Materials to Market Products

The SAP material number and the external market product code may follow different naming conventions. Therefore, SAP needs a mapping mechanism to identify the correct market data for each material.

When a material is entered in the sales order, the custom pricing logic derives the relevant material identifier and uses the configured mapping rules to determine the corresponding external product code.

The system then retrieves the price records associated with that product code.

In scenarios where a material's price depends on multiple market products, the applicable business formula must also be determined from the mapping configuration.

This mapping step is essential because selecting the wrong product code would result in an incorrect base price, even if the average calculation itself is correct.

6. Implementing the Logic in SAP SD Pricing

The automatic calculation is implemented using a custom VOFM alternative calculation routine assigned to condition type PR00 in the relevant pricing procedure.

The high-level implementation steps are:

1. Identify the sales document types and pricing procedure for which automatic pricing is required.
2. Configure the material-to-market-product mapping and the applicable calculation rules.
3. Read the latest five available price records for the relevant product code from the custom table.
4. Calculate the daily midpoint using the high and low values for each date.
5. Calculate the five-day average of the daily midpoints.
6. Apply any additional product-specific calculation rules, where applicable.
7. Return the calculated amount to PR00 during sales order pricing.

The routine is assigned to the alternative calculation type field for PR00 in pricing procedure configuration (transaction V/08).

As a result, the base price is calculated during sales order pricing rather than requiring the user to maintain it manually for every order.

7. Sales Order Processing

Once the configuration and routine are in place, the process works as follows:

1. The background job refreshes the market price data in SAP.
2. The user creates a sales order and enters the relevant material.
3. SAP determines the pricing procedure and processes condition type PR00.
4. The custom routine identifies the market product code and reads the required price history.
5. SAP calculates the five-day average and populates PR00 with the resulting price.
6. The user reviews the proposed price and can manually override it if permitted by the condition configuration.
7. The sales order is saved, and subsequent delivery and billing processes continue according to the existing configuration.

8. Important Considerations

When implementing a similar solution, the following points should be validated:

  • Data availability: Define what should happen if fewer than five valid daily price records are available.
  • Price freshness: Ensure the background job completes successfully before the price is required for sales order creation.
  • Product mapping: Validate that each relevant SAP material maps to the correct external product code.
  • Currency and unit of measure: Confirm that market prices and SAP condition values use compatible currencies and units, or apply the necessary conversions.
  • Rounding: Align the calculation precision and rounding rules with the business requirement.
  • Error handling: Define the expected behaviour when market data is missing, invalid, or unavailable.
  • Manual override: Confirm whether users are allowed to change the calculated PR00 value and how subsequent pricing recalculations should behave.

These checks help ensure that the automation remains reliable when market data or business conditions change.

Conclusion

Automating material pricing in SAP SD can reduce manual effort and improve the consistency of sales order pricing when market prices change frequently.

By combining a scheduled market data update, a custom price history table, a rolling five-day average calculation, and a VOFM alternative calculation routine for PR00, SAP can determine the base price automatically during sales order creation.

The key to a successful implementation is not only the average calculation, but also reliable market data integration, correct material mapping, appropriate pricing configuration, and clear handling of exceptions.

entry.title: Integrating AI into the Order-to-Cash Process
entry.content:
Innovating Order-to-Cash Teaching with AI

The Order-to-Cash (O2C) process in #SAP S/4HAN represents one of the most important end-to-end business processes in an organization by cutting across multiple business functions—sales, marketing, supply chain, logistics, finance and customer service.. A typical O2C process can be represented as:

Customer Inquiry → Quotation → Sales Order → Availability/ATP → Delivery → Picking & Packing → Goods Issue → Billing → Accounts Receivable → Payment

With O2C process students need to understand why each activity is performed, how information flows across functions, how one decision affects subsequent activities, and how the process ultimately contributes to customer service and business performance.

Students need to understand not only the individual steps but also questions such as:

  • Why is a quotation created before a sales order?
  • Is it necessary to create Inquiry and/or Quotation for creating Sales Order?
  • What information flows from the sales order to delivery?
  • What happens when sufficient inventory is not available?
  • Why does goods issue affect inventory and accounting?
  • How does billing create a financial transaction?
  • What happens to the customer's receivable after billing?
  • What business consequences arise when delivery is delayed?

AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot can be integrated at each of these learning points to enhance learning. AI can therefore be positioned as a learning companion around the SAP system, rather than as a replacement for SAP practice. Before entering the system, students can use ChatGPT to explore an Order-to-Cash business scenario, identify relevant process steps and formulate questions that they should investigate in SAP. During the exercise, they can use AI to explore alternative explanations for issues such as incomplete order confirmations, delivery delays, pricing discrepancies or blocked orders. After completing the SAP process, students can use AI to interpret the resulting information, analyse Order-to-Cash data, construct management summaries and reflect on the business implications of their decisions. In this way, AI can help create a continuous learning cycle: understand → investigate → execute → analyse → question → reflect.

The integration of AI also provides an opportunity to make students more actively engaged with SAP by presenting managerial challenges like: A strategic customer requires urgent delivery, but the requested quantity cannot be fully confirmed. What could be causing the problem? What information would you investigate? What alternatives could the company consider? Students can use AI to generate hypotheses, investigate those hypotheses in SAP S/4HANA, use Copilot to analyse relevant data, and then defend their conclusions. The SAP system becomes the evidence base, while AI becomes a tool for exploration and reasoning.

This approach also allows faculty to introduce AI-supported experiential learning into SAP courses. AI tool like ChatGPT can generate different customer and business scenarios, role-play customers or sales managers, create troubleshooting situations and challenge students with follow-up questions. Copilot can support data analysis, visualization and preparation of management-oriented reports using Order-to-Cash data. Students can consequently move from repetitive transaction execution to activities such as diagnosing process problems, comparing alternative decisions, interpreting data and communicating recommendations.

The role of AI, therefore, is not simply to make SAP learning faster or easier. Its greater educational potential lies in shifting the focus from "Can the student execute the transaction correctly?" to broader questions such as "Does the student understand the business process?", "Can the student diagnose what is happening?", "Can the student use data and AI critically?", and "Can the student translate SAP information into a managerial decision?"

Such an approach transforms O2C from a largely transaction-oriented practical exercise into a business simulation and decision-learning experience. Students still develop the essential hands-on SAP skills, but they also develop AI literacy, analytical thinking, problem-solving, business-process understanding and managerial judgment. The objective is not to have AI perform the student's SAP work; rather, it is to use AI to make the student more curious, more analytical and more engaged with the business problem that lies behind the transaction.

 

Some Examples of AI Prompt for O2C Process

  • Act as an SAP business process consultant and ask AI tool to explain the Order-to-Cash process in SAP S/4HANA to an MBA student who understands basic sales and accounting but has never used SAP. Explain the business purpose of each major step and how information flows from one step to another.
  • Asking AI to explain how a sales order, delivery, goods issue, billing document and accounting document are related in an SAP S/4HANA Order-to-Cash process. Give a simple business example
  • Gave students a 3-page customer contract PDF. Ask them to use AI tool to extract SAP SD configuration requirements, create the customer master, and process the order in the live system within defined time frame. Write a summary of learnings.
  • Why can a sales order be created even when the requested quantity is not immediately available?
  • What is the business significance of the delivery block in an O2C process?
  • What could happen to customer satisfaction, inventory and revenue recognition if goods issue is delayed?
  • What happens to the customer's outstanding receivable?
  • A customer order for 500 units has been created, but only 300 units are confirmed for delivery. Identify possible business and SAP-related reasons and explain how a consultant should investigate the issue.
  • Generate five different Order-to-Cash business scenarios for an MBA SAP class. Each scenario should involve a different customer, product, quantity, delivery requirement and business problem. Ensure that the scenarios require students to analyze the implications for sales order, delivery, inventory and billing.
  • A customer has placed an order for 2,000 units. Only 1,200 units are available, the customer has a strict delivery deadline, and the sales manager wants to maximize customer satisfaction without creating excessive inventory pressure. Analyze the situation and recommend how the O2C process should be managed.

 

AI can help in improving Learning Outcomes

  • On-Demand Clarification: Students stuck on why a process steps to be followed in a certain order can ask AI rather than waiting for the next class.
  • Active, Not Passive Learning: Instead of memorizing process sequences, students can use AI to build their own models from SAP export – reinforcing the “Why” behind each transaction.
  • Document-heavy Scenarios Made Traceable: Real Business scenarios involve contracts, RFQs, and invoices. AI allows students practice with realistic, messy documents rather than oversimplified examples.
  • Cross-function thinking: Students can use AI to get clear understanding of cross-functional integrated system process used by O-2-C of SAP.
  • Scenario Variation: Faculty can use AI tool to generate number of different scenarios with varied terms – giving every student a different case and reducing copy-paste submissions.
  • Error-Injection: Faculty can use AI to inject a deliberate errors into a dataset forcing students to identify and correct --- this helps in assessing diagnostic skills.

 

Conclusion

  • The Order-to-Cash process provides an excellent environment for integrating generative AI into SAP education because it combines business processes, transactional data, cross-functional dependencies and managerial decisions.
  • AI tools like ChatGPT can serve as a conceptual tutor, questioning partner, scenario generator and troubleshooting companion, while Microsoft Copilot can add significant value when students work with Excel, PowerPoint, Word and other Microsoft 365-based learning activities and O2C datasets.
  • The ultimate objective, however, should not be to teach students to use AI to complete SAP assignments faster. It should be to teach them to combine AI, SAP and human judgment effectively.

entry.title: Unlock Your KPI Insights Instantly with SAP Joule: Introducing the Smart Business KPI Capability

The Problem Every Business User Knows

Your company tracks dozens of KPIs. They're spread across finance, procurement, and operations — each living inside a different Fiori app, behind a different tile, reached through a different set of clicks. Every morning you navigate the same menus to find the same reports. The data is there. Getting to it is just... slow.

The Smart Business KPI (SSB KPI) Capability brings your performance dashboards directly into Joule's conversational interface. Ask a plain-language question — get a clickable, navigable KPI card back, right inside the chat pane.

No new configuration. No new data models. The Smart Business KPI capability connects directly to your existing setup.

Take an Accounts Receivable Manager who needs to check Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) and related collection KPIs at the start of each day. Previously: open the Fiori Launchpad, locate the AR overview tile, navigate into the report.

"Show me my assigned KPIs" · "List my KPIs" · "What KPIs do I have?"

Joule retrieves all Smart Business KPIs assigned to your user role — regardless of threshold status — and presents them in a KPI Overview card. Each item is a direct deep link: one click opens the KPI's runtime report in the correct Fiori application, with the evaluation context already applied.

Why It Matters

Zero navigation overhead

No need to remember which tile leads to which KPI. Just ask.

Role-relevant results only

You see exactly what you're assigned — nothing more, nothing less.

One click to live data

Every KPI card item deep-links to the runtime report with evaluation context pre-loaded.

Works in 40+ languages

Full localization including Arabic, Hebrew, Japanese, Chinese, and all major European languages.

Secure by design

Data retrieval uses your existing SSO session — users see only what they're already entitled to see.

No extra setup

Connects to your existing Smart Business KPI setup with no new data modeling required.

When you ask Joule about your KPIs, it understands your intent, retrieves the relevant Smart Business KPIs using your existing SSO authentication, and formats them into a UI5 Integration Card native to the Joule interface.

Every item in the card carries Intent-Based Navigation (IBN) links — the KPI's Semantic Object, Action, and Evaluation or Report ID are embedded as parameters, so one click opens the exact right Fiori application with the exact right context.

Try it today: Ask Joule "Show me my assigned KPIs" in your SAP S/4HANA Cloud 2612 environment. We'd love to hear how it fits your workflow — share your experience in the comments.

entry.title: HighRadius vs. SAP FSCM: Hard-Earned Lessons from a Global Cosmetics S/4HANA Transformation
entry.content:
As consumer goods and beauty organizations accelerate their digital finance transformations, the debate surrounding Accounts Receivable (AR) optimization often gets reduced to a binary question: Should we use native SAP Financial Supply Chain Management (FSCM) or replace it with a specialized cloud solution like HighRadius? Over an 18-year career leading global SAP transformations across Europe, Asia, and the Middle East, I have watched finance executives repeatedly fall into the trap of treating this as an "either/or" software selection choice.

The reality on the ground is completely different. When you move past the product brochures and slide decks, you discover that the most successful global templates do not choose between them. Instead, they treat SAP as the core transactional engine and HighRadius as an intelligent edge layer. Achieving this coexistence, however, requires navigating complex architectural integration points, version-specific database behaviors, and industry-specific commercial nuances—such as complex trade promotions and massive retail deductions—that software vendors rarely mention during the sales cycle.

The Friction Point: Why Pure SAP FSCM Fell Short in Global Beauty & Cosmetics Rollouts

To understand where native capabilities hit their limits, we can look at a global cosmetics leader's rollout running on an SAP S/4HANA 2023 On-Premises environment with Feature Package Stack 02 (FPS02). The business model managed a deeply fragmented customer landscape: massive multinational retail networks (such as Sephora, Ulta, and major department stores), thousands of highly localized salon accounts, and high-volume e-commerce payment clearing.

Initially, the steering committee pushed for a pure SAP FSCM Collections and Dispute Management implementation to minimize their software footprint and leverage their existing licensing. However, as we entered the blueprinting and prototyping phases, the operational limitations of a purely rule-based system in the cosmetics industry became apparent:

  • The Trade Promotion Deduction Avalanche: Major retail beauty chains routinely short-pay invoices based on cooperative advertising agreements, volume rebates, and markdown allowances. In standard SAP FSCM, these deductions flood the subledger as individual residual open items. Dispute specialists spent up to 40% of their day manually linking these short payments to promotional agreements, creating a massive operational backlog.
  • Static Collection Strategies: SAP FSCM generates collection worklists based on static, pre-defined rules—such as aging buckets, risk categories, and total open values. In a fast-moving retail consumer landscape, these rigid rules created bottlenecks. The system flooded collection specialists with alerts for large, stable retail accounts that routinely paid according to strict corporate payment cycles, while high-risk, deteriorating independent salon behaviors slipped through unnoticed because they hadn't crossed a specific net-due threshold.
  • The Analytics Deficit: Standard SAP operational reporting (even via custom operational data provisioning views or standard Fiori FES 2023 apps) provided lagging operational KPIs. The business leadership lacked predictive cash forecasting and granular, dynamic Day Sales Outstanding (DSO) trend analysis segmented by shifting channel behavior patterns (D2C vs. B2B Wholesale).

The organization realized that while FSCM was perfectly engineered to maintain the financial integrity of the ledger, it lacked the algorithmic agility needed to optimize cash application hit rates and automatically resolve multi-brand deduction claims. This realization shifted our strategy to a hybrid architecture deploying the HighRadius Cash Application Cloud and Deduction Management System (DMS) modules alongside our SAP core.

Architectural Reality: Orchestrating Integration via Hyperion Integration Platform (HIP)

Integrating a multi-entity S/4HANA 2023 core with a cloud-based Autonomous Finance platform is rarely a "plug-and-play" exercise. For this transformation, we built a hybrid ecosystem where SAP functioned strictly as the immutable system of record, while HighRadius operated as the system of engagement and intelligence, orchestrated via the Hyperion Integration Platform (HIP) as the corporate middleware layer.

The underlying architecture relied on standardizing data exchange protocols across an enterprise footprint. Because the corporate landscape utilized HIP as its centralized enterprise middleware, we funneled all transactional deltas, ledger extract files, and incoming bank lockbox information through this layer to perform essential schema transformations before delivering them to High Radius.

The technical complexity surfaced heavily during the orchestration of the data loop between HighRadius Cash App, DMS, and SAP FI-AR via HIP:

  1. The Cash App Ingestion: HighRadius Cash App automatically extracts unstructured remittance data via OCR from customer emails and retail vendor portals, matching payments against open customer line items. This open item subledger data is periodically extracted from SAP operational views (such as BSID) and delivered through HIP as a structured outbound file payload.
  2. The DMS Splitting Mechanism: When a retail client short-pays an invoice due to a trade promotion dispute, the Cash App module flags the variance and automatically routes the residual shortage amount to the HighRadius DMS module.
  3. Automated Inbound Postings through HIP: Once a deduction is classified in the cloud, HighRadius communicates the clearing parameters back down. HIP intercepts this response payload, translates the cloud parameters into SAP-compatible structures, and executes an inbound transactional interface leveraging standard functions like BAPI_ACC_DOCUMENT_POST. This automatically clears the original invoice line item in S/4HANA, posts a residual open item for the short-payment, and maps specific SAP Reason Codes corresponding to the dispute type (e.g., Pricing, Shortage, or Coop Ad).

By utilizing HIP as the unified integration layer, we eliminated complex point-to-point interface sprawl, ensuring that our daily cash application cycle remained decoupled from the extended timelines required to research and settle retail trade promotions.

Version Constraints and Unexpected Implementation Roadblocks

Moving from conceptual architecture to actual deployment on S/4HANA 2023 (FPS02) exposed several technical constraints that project planners frequently overlook.

Our first major hurdle involved the Universal Journal (ACDOCA). In older SAP ERP Central Component (ECC) environments, financial data was highly segmented across index tables (like BSID and BSAD). S/4HANA’s unified ACDOCA design vastly speeds up internal reporting, but extracting massive delta datasets of open and cleared items to feed external machine learning models can degrade system performance if not carefully managed.

During initial data cycles, our delta extraction queries for historical customer payment behaviors began causing severe memory bottlenecks in the SAP HANA database due to the sheer volume of line items generated by cosmetic wholesale shipments. We had to configure the SAP extraction jobs and HIP to abandon generic open-ended queries and completely redesign our extraction logic. We restricted data pulls to strict timestamp-based delta captures leveraging specialized SAP Change Data Capture (CDC) mechanisms, ensuring that data replication to HighRadius occurred in controlled micro-batches outside of peak financial closing windows.

Another critical constraint appeared within the Business Partner (BP) master data synchronization. Because this was a global program spanning multiple geographies and brands, the client utilized complex BP groupings with varying field modification rules across different company codes. HighRadius requires a highly standardized payload for its ingestion models.

We encountered repeated integration errors where localized fields in SAP (such as specific regional tax classification rules or localized payment block reasons) caused data validation rejections in the HighRadius staging tables. This required a comprehensive data-cleansing initiative and configuring specialized transformation rules within HIP to map heterogeneous SAP BP attributes into a unified schema that the HighRadius machine learning algorithms could accurately interpret.

The Measurable Bottom Line: Concrete Project Outcomes

The true validation of this hybrid architectural strategy lies in the quantifiable business results achieved in 12 months of post-go-live. By shifting from static, rule-based workflows to an AI-driven, predictive model, the global shared services organization transformed its balance sheet performance:

 

The dramatic leap in our auto-cash application hit rate was particularly impactful for the consumer goods model. By leveraging HighRadius’s OCR and machine learning algorithms to automatically parse unstructured remittance advices from customer emails and retail vendor portals, the system matched payments to open items in S/4HANA without human intervention. This freed up our senior credit analysts to focus exclusively on negotiating complex promotional shortages rather than manual data entry.

Strategic Recommendations for Enterprise Architects Today

If I were to approach a global cosmetics architecture rollout again today, I would change my implementation strategy in two distinct areas:

  1. Mandate Early-Stage Data Cleansing: Do not wait for the integration testing phase to discover that your SAP Business Partner master data or customer hierarchies are inconsistent across regions. Master data remediation must be treated as a strict technical prerequisite that runs six months before any external cloud integration work begins.
  2. Enforce the Transactional Boundaries Immediately: Be incredibly disciplined about keeping business logic where it belongs. Cloud platforms will tempt you to build complex custom validation workflows or store trade promotion contracts within their environments. Resist this pressure. All accounting principles, credit limits, and final clearing rules must reside strictly within the S/4HANA core to protect your financial system of record. Use the HIP-enabled cloud edge purely for execution speed, prediction, and user experience.

Ultimately, the choice between SAP FSCM and HighRadius is a false dichotomy. The real challenge—and the real opportunity for enterprise architects—lies in configuring a robust, high-performing integration framework that respects the transactional authority of SAP while fully unleashing the analytical power of autonomous finance.

Author Bio

Prakashreddy Bodireddy is an SAP S/4HANA Certified FICO Solution Architect with 18+ years of experience delivering global finance transformation programs across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and the Americas. His expertise includes SAP S/4HANA Finance, FSCM,  Group Reporting, IFRS15/RAR, Treasury, and HighRadius integration.

entry.title: SAP BAIP Kyma runtime 正式落地中国：扩展云原生开发能力
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 现已在中国正式上线，在本地 SAP BAIP 上提供了一个托管 Kubernetes 运行时，支持云原生应用、微服务及 SAP 扩展开发。

云原生创新能力走近中国客户

现代企业越来越需要在不增加核心系统复杂度的前提下，扩展业务应用、连接各类系统、并持续交付新的数字化能力。

SAP BAIP 在中国已提供 Cloud Foundry runtime 作为成熟的 PaaS 选项，适用于基于 buildpack 工作流的应用部署。Kyma runtime 则面向不同的需求场景。它基于开源 Kyma 项目和 Kubernetes 构建，让开发团队可以直接使用容器化工作负载、Serverless Functions 以及更广泛的 Kubernetes 生态系统——不限编程语言和框架。任何可容器化的工作负载均可在 Kyma runtime 上运行。

2026 年 6 月 2 日，SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）率先上线，随后于 2026 年 7 月 10 日扩展至中国（上海）——通过本地 BTPEA 商业模式，在两个区域全面开放。

现已提供哪些内容？

该服务基于 BTPEA 商业模式提供，SKU 为 8016044（面向客户的 BTPEA SKU），包含以下服务计划：

服务名称服务计划名称可用数据中心
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Alibaba Cloud中国（上海）— cn40
Kyma RuntimeKyma Runtime Azure中国（华北3）— cn20

客户和合作伙伴可通过 SAP Discovery Center 查看服务及其可用地区：

  • 中国（华北3）— Kyma runtime
  • 中国（上海）— Kyma runtime

中国 BTPEA 价格表中列出了 SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 的 Standard 计费计划。

为何重要

托管、灵活的云原生应用基础平台

自建 Kubernetes 需要持续投入集群管理、版本升级、安全补丁和基础设施运维。SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime 消除了这一负担：SAP 负责底层平台的管理，客户则完全掌控自己的应用和工作负载。开发团队可以专注于构建业务能力，而不是维护基础设施。

与 Cloud Foundry runtime 相比，Kyma 提供了一种截然不同的开发模式。Cloud Foundry 通过 buildpack 对运行时进行抽象，这种方式非常适合快速部署 Java 或 Node.js 应用，但对能运行什么、如何运行有一定限制。Kyma 没有这类约束：无论使用何种语言或框架，任何容器化工作负载都可以在 Kyma 上运行，团队还可以直接使用 Kubernetes 原生工具链——包括用于打包的 Helm、自定义资源定义、精细化资源配置，以及更广泛的 CNCF 生态系统。对于构建现代云原生应用或需要精确控制工作负载的团队而言，这种灵活性是显著的优势。

两种运行时相辅相成。Cloud Foundry 仍然是 buildpack 应用部署的可靠选择；当团队需要容器原生的灵活性、多语言支持或 Kubernetes 生态工具时，Kyma 则更为适合。

通过事件驱动集成扩展 SAP 应用

Kyma runtime 内置了 Eventing 组件，允许应用直接订阅来自 SAP S/4HANA 及其他 SAP 系统的业务事件——扩展程序可以实时响应销售订单创建、货物移动或主数据变更等事件，无需轮询或点对点连接。由于该能力已集成在运行时中，团队无需单独配置消息服务即可开始构建事件驱动扩展。

结合 Serverless Functions 和内置 API Gateway，这使得构建轻量、松耦合的扩展程序变得切实可行——这些扩展与 SAP 核心系统并行运行，而非嵌入其中。自定义逻辑独立演进，升级周期解耦，核心系统保持稳定。

对于超出 SAP 间集成范畴的场景——连接第三方系统、编排多步骤工作流或构建全新业务应用——Kyma 提供了同样的 Kubernetes 基础平台，并具备灵活引入任何所需服务或技术的能力。

扩展本地 SAP BAIP 开发组合

随着 Kyma runtime 在中国（华北3）和中国（上海）相继上线，中国客户在 SAP BAIP 上多了一个可用的运行时选择。

对于正在构建容器化应用、API 集成、事件驱动扩展或微服务的团队，这一选项尤为实用。

Kyma runtime 的上线拓宽了中国生态系统可用的技术选择，为云原生应用开发提供了又一个坚实基础。

entry.title: Bringing SAP BAIP, Kyma Runtime to China: Expanding Cloud-Native Development Capabilities
entry.content:
SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is now available in China, extending the local SAP BAIP portfolio with a managed Kubernetes-based runtime for cloud-native applications, microservices, and SAP extensions.

Bringing Cloud-Native Innovation Closer to Chinese Customers

Modern enterprises increasingly need to extend business applications, connect systems, and deliver new digital capabilities without introducing unnecessary complexity into their core landscapes.

SAP BAIP in China already offers Cloud Foundry runtime as a mature PaaS option for deploying applications using buildpack-based workflows. Kyma runtime addresses a different set of needs. Built on the open-source Kyma project and Kubernetes, it gives development teams direct access to container-based workloads, serverless functions, and the broader Kubernetes ecosystem—without restriction on programming language or framework. Any workload that can be containerized can run on Kyma runtime.

On June 2, 2026, SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime became available in China (North 3), followed by China (Shanghai) on July 10, 2026—making this managed cloud-native application runtime available through the local BTPEA commercial offering across both regions.

What Is Now Available?

SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime is offered under the BTPEA commercial model, under SKU 8016044 (the customer-facing BTPEA SKU), with the following service plans:

  • China (North 3) — Kyma Runtime
  • China (Shanghai) — Kyma Runtime

The China BTPEA price list lists the Standard plan as a billable plan for SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime.

Why This Matters

A Managed, Flexible Foundation for Cloud-Native Applications

Running Kubernetes in-house requires ongoing investment in cluster management, upgrades, security patching, and infrastructure operations. SAP BAIP, Kyma runtime removes that burden: SAP manages the underlying platform, while customers retain full control over their applications and workloads. Development teams can focus on building business capabilities instead of maintaining infrastructure.

Compared to Cloud Foundry runtime, Kyma offers a meaningfully different development model. Cloud Foundry abstracts the runtime through buildpacks, which works well for deploying Java or Node.js applications quickly but limits what you can run and how. Kyma places no such constraints: any containerized workload runs on Kyma regardless of language or framework, and teams have direct access to Kubernetes-native tooling—Helm for packaging, custom resource definitions, fine-grained resource configuration, and the broader CNCF ecosystem. For teams building modern cloud-native applications or needing precise control over their workloads, this flexibility is a significant advantage.

The two runtimes are complementary. Cloud Foundry remains a solid choice for buildpack-based application deployment; Kyma is the better fit when container-native flexibility, polyglot development, or Kubernetes ecosystem tooling is a requirement.

Extending SAP Applications with Event-Driven Integration

Kyma runtime includes a built-in Eventing component that allows applications to subscribe directly to business events from SAP S/4HANA and other SAP systems—so an extension can react to a sales order creation, a goods movement, or a master data change in real time, without polling or point-to-point connections. Having this capability integrated into the runtime means teams can start building event-driven extensions without separately provisioning and configuring a messaging service.

Combined with serverless functions and a built-in API Gateway, this makes it practical to build lightweight, loosely coupled extensions that sit alongside the SAP core rather than inside it. Custom logic evolves independently, upgrade cycles are decoupled, and the core system remains stable.

For scenarios that go beyond SAP-to-SAP integration—connecting third-party systems, orchestrating multi-step workflows, or building net-new business applications—Kyma provides the same Kubernetes-based foundation with the flexibility to incorporate any service or technology the use case requires.

Expanding the Local SAP BAIP Development Portfolio

With Kyma runtime available in China (North 3) and China (Shanghai), customers gain an additional runtime option within the local SAP BAIP portfolio.

This is particularly relevant for teams building containerized applications, API-based integrations, event-driven extensions, and microservices that complement SAP business solutions.

The availability of Kyma runtime broadens the technology choices available to the China ecosystem and provides another foundation for cloud-native application development.

entry.title: SAP PLMSI & Clean Core
entry.content:
– Positioning PLM System Integration within the Clean Core Extensibility Model

Clean Core is a central architectural principle of SAP that aims to keep the SAP core as close to the standard as possible. Extensions should be implemented exclusively through released, upgrade-stable interfaces and extension points. This ensures that system upgrades can be carried out smoothly and that customer-specific adaptations remain maintainable and future-proof in the long term.

In the context of SAP PLM System Integration (PLMSI), the standardized integration component for bidirectional data transfer between SAP S/4HANA and an external PLM system (e.g. Siemens Teamcenter), the question arises as to how customer-specific extensions can be implemented in a clean-core-compliant manner.

This Block-Post explains the clean core extensibility levels, positions the PLMSI extension mechanisms within this framework, and provides clear guidance for implementation practice.

Contents

  1. The SAP Clean Core Extensibility Model
  2. Extension Patterns: On-Stack and Side-by-Side
  3. SAP PLMSI in the Context Clean Core
    3.1 BAdIs as Released Extension Points
    3.2 Categories of PLMSI BAdIs
    3.3 Configuration vs. Implementation
  4. Positioning PLMSI Extensions with Clean Core Levels
  5. Future-Proofing and Evolution
  6. Conclusion

 

1. The SAP Clean Core Extensibility Model

SAP defines four extensibility levels (A through D) that describe the degree of clean core compliance of an extension. The higher the level, the more upgrade-stable and future-proof the implementation.

Level

Description

Clean Core?

Level A

Extensions based on released APIs and extension points. Development with ABAP Cloud (SAP Build) or side-by-side on SAP BTP. Highest upgrade stability.

✅Yes – Target state

Level B

Extensions using classic APIs and frameworks (e.g. BAPIs, classic BAdIs) that are not formally tagged as "released" but are recognized as upgrade-stable.

✅Yes

Level C

Use of internal SAP objects that are not officially released. Conditionally clean, provided that change-log monitoring is set up.

⚠️Conditional

Level D

Modifications, implicit enhancements, direct table writes, or non-recommended extension technologies. Not upgrade-stable.

❌No

The following diagram shows how clean core levels map to SAP standard objects:

Figure 1: Clean core levels mapped to SAP standard objects
Source: SAP – Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud (2024)

2. Extension Patterns: On-Stack and Side-by-Side

SAP distinguishes two fundamental extension patterns for SAP Cloud ERP Private:

A) On-Stack Extensibility (directly on SAP S/4HANA):

  • Adapting and extending standard applications (e.g. custom fields, data model extensions)
  • Creating custom full-stack applications with custom UI, application logic, and persistence
  • Creating and consuming APIs and events for integration connectivity

B) Side-by-Side Extensibility (on SAP Business Technology Platform):

  • Developing custom full-stack or mobile applications
  • Automating tasks and processes across system boundaries
  • Using workflows, rules, and central entry points

The following diagram provides an overview of the extension patterns:

Figure 2: Extension use case patterns for SAP Cloud ERP Private
Source: SAP – Clean core extensibility for SAP S/4HANA Cloud (2024)

3. SAP PLMSI in the Context of Clean Core

3.1 BAdIs as Released Extension Points

SAP PLM System Integration (PLMSI) provides a wide range of documented BAdIs (Business Add-Ins) that are designated as official extension points for customer-specific adaptations. These BAdIs are documented in the SAP Configuration Guide for PLMSI and therefore belong to the released extension points of the SAP standard.

The use of these BAdIs is clean-core-compliant and corresponds to Level A or Level B of the SAP extensibility model, provided that only released or classic APIs and objects are used within the BAdI implementation.

3.2 Categories of PLMSI BAdIs

The PLMSI BAdIs can be categorized as follows:

Post-Processing BAdIs: Customer-specific post-processing steps after successful standard processing of inbound messages (e.g. for material master, document master, change objects, bills of material).

Read Extension Fields BAdIs: Enrichment of outbound data with additional customer-specific fields during read access (e.g. BAdI /PLMF/BD_PV_READ_EXTN_FLD for material master data).

Custom Conversion BAdIs: Definition of custom conversion logic for data formats (e.g. date formats, units of measure).

Custom Logic BAdIs: Complete implementation of custom processing logic as a replacement for the standard integration. These BAdIs offer methods for Maintain (write) and Read (read) and allow the creation of entirely custom SAP objects or the implementation of deviating business logic.

Selection Condition BAdIs: Adaptation of selection conditions for specific object types (e.g. routings).

Inbound Request BAdIs: Adjustment of data in inbound maintain requests before standard processing, as well as modification of the response before it is returned to the external system.

Note: The number of avialabe BAdI extention points varies depending on the PLMSI version and feature pack. 

3.3 Configuration vs. Implementation

A significant portion of PLMSI functionality can be covered purely through configuration – without any code development. This includes, among other things, scenario definitions, attribute mappings, conversion rules, and the assignment of processing pipelines.

For requirements beyond this – such as complex business logic, customer-specific validations, or the integration of additional SAP objects – the BAdIs described above are available. This combination of configuration and BAdI-based extension is architecturally intentional and fully clean-core-compliant.

4. Positioning PLMSI Extensions within Clean Core Levels

Extension Type

Clean Core Level

Assessment

PLMSI configuration (scenario setup, attribute mappings, conversion rules)

Level A

✅Fully compliant

BAdI implementation using released/classic APIs and objects

Level A / B

✅Compliant

BAdI implementation using internal SAP objects

Level C

⚠️Conditionally compliant – change-log monitoring recommended

Direct modification of SAP standard (not recommended)

Level D

❌Not compliant

5. Future-Proofing and Evolution

Since the PLMSI BAdIs are provided as released extension points, upgrade safety is should be ensured. SAP updates typically do not affect BAdI implementations, as the BAdI framework ensures a clean separation between standard code and customer extensions.

Furthermore, it is possible that future PLMSI versions may incorporate into the standard some extensions that are currently realized through BAdIs. This would prospectively reduce customer-specific implementation effort and further increase the degree of standardization.

SAP regularly releases new released APIs and BAdIs. For a current overview, the following resources are recommended:

  • SAP Road Map Explorer for PLM System Integration
  • SAP Business Accelerator Hub (for released APIs)
  • Cloudification Repository Viewer (for classic APIs)
  • SAP Help Portal – PLMSI Configuration Guide

6. Conclusion

The use of SAP PLMSI BAdIs is clean-core-compliant. SAP has intentionally provided these extension points to enable customer-specific integration requirements within a future-proof, upgrade-stable architectural framework.

For implementation, the following clear recommendations apply:

  • Prioritize configuration – wherever possible, address requirements through PLMSI configuration.
  • Use BAdIs with released objects – this corresponds to Level A/B and is unconditionally clean-core-compliant.
  • Use internal objects only when necessary – and set up change-log monitoring in that case (Level C).
  • Avoid modifications – direct interventions in the SAP standard are not clean-core-compliant and jeopardize upgrade capability (Level D).

https://www.sap.com/documents/2024/09/20aece06-d87e-0010-bca6-c68f7e60039b.html

entry.title: Recap der Kaffee-Ecke: Gemini Notebook im SAP Learning Hub – KI-gestütztes und barrierefreies Lernen
entry.content:
Am 15. Oktober traf sich die SAP Training und Change Community zur monatlichen Kaffee-Ecke - dieses Mal rund um ein Tool, das vielen noch unter dem alten Namen bekannt ist: NotebookLM. Gleich zu Beginn wurde klargestellt: Das Tool heißt inzwischen Gemini Notebook. Anna Dostert und Cara Damm von Google zeigten live, wie es im SAP Learning Hub integriert ist, welche Lernformate es mitbringt und wo SAP bewusst Grenzen gesetzt hat, die in der generischen Version nicht existieren.

NotebookLM wird zu Gemini Notebook

Was viele aus früheren Demos noch als NotebookLM kennen, ist inzwischen offiziell Teil des Gemini-Stacks von Google und heißt entsprechend Gemini Notebook. Beide Bezeichnungen kursieren noch im Alltag; in dieser Session – wie auch in der Praxis – meinen sie dasselbe Tool.

Grundprinzip: Antworten nur aus vertrauenswürdigen Quellen

 

Gemini Notebook zieht seine Inhalte ausschließlich aus vorab festgelegten Quellen. Fragen, Zusammenfassungen und alle weiteren Ausgabeformate entstehen nur auf Basis dieser Quellen.

Wird eine Information dort nicht gefunden, bleibt die Antwort offen. Quellenverweise machen jede Ausgabe bis zur genauen Dokumentstelle nachvollziehbar.

Im SAP Learning Hub wird für jeden Kurs ein eigenes Notebook eingerichtet, mit den jeweiligen Kurseinheiten als Quellen. Das Tool greift ausschließlich auf kursrelevante Inhalte zu.

Lernformate für verschiedene Präferenzen

 

Was Gemini Notebook von einem einfachen Chat unterscheidet, ist die Bandbreite der Ausgaben. Die Audioübersicht ist als Gespräch zwischen zwei Protagonisten aufgebaut – ähnlich einem Podcast. Über eine Join-Funktion lässt sich während der Wiedergabe eine Frage stellen, die das Notebook direkt beantwortet.

Weitere Ausgabeformate sind Mindmaps zur Kursnavigation, aus denen direkt in relevante Themenbereiche gesprungen werden kann, sowie Study-Guides für die Prüfungsvorbereitung, FAQs, Briefing-Dokumente und Infografiken.

Damit steht eine Bandbreite an visuellen, textbasierten und auditiven Formaten bereit, die verschiedene Lernpräferenzen bedienen. Die Audioübersicht und die Chat-Funktion sprechen darüber hinaus dialogorientierte Lernpräferenzen an.

Diese Formatvielfalt hat eine direkte Relevanz für barrierefreies Lernen. Wo klassische Kursmaterialien oft text- oder folienbasiert vorliegen, liefert Gemini Notebook dieselben Inhalte als Audioübersicht, Mindmap oder interaktiven Chat. Wie Anna Dostert in der Session betonte: Visuelle, textbasierte und auditive Lernpräferenzen werden damit gleichermaßen bedient.

Zur Frage nach Quizzen: Eine Quiz-Funktion gibt es als Studio-Ausgabe. Per direkter Chat-Anweisung lässt sich außerdem jederzeit ein Quiz für den Gesamtkontext oder ein bestimmtes Kapitel erstellen. Ob das Studio-Format auch im kontrollierten Learning-Hub-Kontext bereitsteht, muss noch geprüft werden.

Unterstützte Quellen und Kapazitäten

 

Gemini Notebook verarbeitet unter anderem Google-Dokumente und -Präsentationen, PDFs, Text- und Markdown-Dateien, Webseiten, Bilder sowie Video- und YouTube-Links. Microsoft-Formate wie Word oder PowerPoint können text- und folienbasiert eingebunden werden, zum Beispiel als PDF-Export.

Große Excel-Tabellen können ebenfalls als PDF-Datei als Quelle genutzt werden, auch wenn die Optik im PDF für User ungewöhnlich ist, für Gemini macht das keinen Unterschied.

Das aktuelle Limit liegt bei rund 300 Quellen pro Notebook und bis zu 500.000 Wörtern pro Quelle. Für sehr umfangreiche Unternehmenswissensbestände ist das Tool nicht ausgelegt – dort sind andere Architekturen (und Tools) sinnvoll.

Datenschutz

 

Kundendaten bleiben unter der Kontrolle der jeweiligen Organisation. Google schützt sie vor unberechtigtem Zugriff und nutzt sie weder für Werbung noch zum Training allgemeiner Modelle oder der Modelle anderer Kunden.

 

Nutzung von Gemini Notebook im SAP Learning Hub

Die Learning-Hub-Integration ist enger gefasst als die Consumer- oder reguläre Enterprise-Version – und das ist keine technische Einschränkung, sondern eine bewusste Entscheidung: SAP kontrolliert darüber die Inhalte, Ausgaben und den Bezug zu Kursinhalten und Zertifizierungszielen.

 

Eigene Unternehmensdokumente, Prozesshandbücher oder Projektnotizen lassen sich im Learning-Hub-Notebook nicht ergänzen. Technisch wäre das außerhalb des Learning Hubs mit einer geeigneten Unternehmenslizenz und einer separaten Gemini-Notebook-Umgebung möglich. Oder eben einer privaten Lizenzierung, die kostenlose Version beinhaltet bis zu 100 Notebooks, 50 Quellen pro Notebook und 50 Chat-Anfragen pro Tag).

Kursinhalte im Audio- oder Videoformat werden von SAP vorab geprüft und freigegeben, um sicherzustellen, dass Lernende die korrekten Lerninhalte zur Verfügung gestellt bekommen.

Der Chatverlauf ist pro Person individuell: Öffnen verschiedene Personen denselben Kurs, ist die Interaktion der anderen Lernenden nicht einsehbar.

Bei aufeinander aufbauenden Kursen kann SAP Recap-Dateien mit Kerninformationen früherer Inhalte hinterlegen. Fehlt diese Information im aktuellen Notebook, muss zum früheren Kurs zurückgekehrt werden – das Tool ergänzt kein Wissen außerhalb seiner Quellen.

Verfügbarkeit und offene Fragen

Für Personen mit Zugang zum SAP Learning Hub ist die Nutzung von Gemini Notebook ohne zusätzliche Einzelbuchung über „Upskill faster with AI" zugänglich.

Eine Übersicht der Kurse, für die Gemini Notebooks aktiviert sind, gibt es aktuell noch nicht. Bei der Erstellung der Notebooks werden aktuell stark nachgefragte Kurse priorisiert.

Für Preferred-Success-Kunden muss noch geprüft werden, ob Gemini Notebook in der Preferred Success Edition freigeschaltet ist. Da es dort hauptsächlich wenige Support Inhalte gibt, ist das eher unwahrscheinlich.

Für SuccessFactors Learning arbeitet SAP an einem ersten Proof of Concept. Einen ersten Einblick gibt der Blogbeitrag: SAP and Google Are Bringing AI-Powered Workspaces to Everyday Work

Ausblick auf die nächste Kaffee Ecke

Neben dem Lernkontext zeigte die Diskussion, dass Gemini Notebook auch für arbeitsbezogene Szenarien relevant ist. Thomas stellte in diesem Zusammenhang Joule for Consultants vor: ein separates KI-Werkzeug, das den Use Case „tun" statt „lernen" abdeckt – also Projektvorbereitung, Fragen zu SAP Activate und die Erstellung von Deliverables. Das führt direkt zum Thema der nächsten Session: Im Januar werden die verschiedenen verfügbaren SAP KI-Werkzeuge vorgestellt und eingeordnet, darunter Joule for Consultants, Joule Work Desktop und Joule Studio.

Anmeldung und aktuelle Termine: go4.events.sap.com/eur-change-training-kaffee-ecke

Häufige Fragen aus der Session

Welche Quellen kann Gemini Notebook verarbeiten? Google-Dokumente, PDFs, Text- und Markdown-Dateien, Webseiten, Bilder und YouTube-Links. Microsoft Word und PowerPoint funktionieren text- und folienbasiert; bei großen Excel-Tabellen empfiehlt sich ein PDF-Export. Das Limit liegt bei rund 300 Quellen pro Notebook und bis zu 500.000 Wörtern pro Quelle.

Können eigene Unternehmensdokumente im SAP Learning Hub ergänzt werden? Nein. Die Learning-Hub-Integration ist auf vorkuratierte Kursinhalte beschränkt. Eigene Dokumente lassen sich nur in einer separaten Gemini-Notebook-Umgebung mit Unternehmenslizenz einbinden.

Ist die Funktion auch für Preferred-Success-Kunden verfügbar? Das wird aktuell noch geprüft. Es gibt unterschiedliche Learning-Hub-Zugänge, die genaue Freischaltung wird nachgereicht.

Wie funktioniert die Audioübersicht? Ähnlich einem Podcast mit zwei Sprechrollen. Über eine Join-Funktion können während der Wiedergabe Fragen gestellt werden, die aus dem Kurskontext beantwortet werden. Die Audioübersicht lässt sich auch unterwegs nutzen, etwa im Zug oder über die Freisprechanlage im Auto.

Wird an einer Integration in SuccessFactors Learning gearbeitet? Ja. SAP arbeitet an einem ersten Proof of Concept. Details dazu stehen im Blogbeitrag SAP and Google Are Bringing AI-Powered Workspaces to Everyday Work.

Wie steht es um den Datenschutz? Kundendaten bleiben unter der Kontrolle der jeweiligen Organisation. Google nutzt sie weder für Werbung noch zum Training allgemeiner Modelle oder der Modelle anderer Kunden.
