entry.title: ACDOCA Partitioning: Plan for Growth Before the Next Downtime Window
entry.content:
Introduction

A growing partition can need attention just when the business can't spare a long outage. The best opportunity to avoid that squeeze is before go-live, when there is still room to test a layout against future growth. Using ACDOCA as the example, I look at that early design decision and the harder choice on an existing system: whether native repartitioning or a staged rebuild with SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server (SLT) can fit the available capacity and business window.

Large tables can become a major operational pain point. In S/4HANA, ACDOCA deserves particular attention because financial posting and reporting depend on it. Review its growth, partition balance and maintenance requirements regularly, before capacity or downtime constraints narrow the options. The same discipline applies to other large SAP HANA tables.

1. Design for growth before go-live

On a new implementation, bring the finance team and HANA administrators into the partition discussion before the bulk load. Estimate journal-line growth, migration volumes, retention and peak posting activity, then test the proposed layout against the reports and business transactions that matter. Give someone responsibility for reviewing growth after go-live. SAP's design guidance calls for testing both select and insert performance as data changes. [1]

Hash partitioning aims to distribute rows across partitions. Range partitioning groups values into intervals, such as periods; its effectiveness depends on the actual distribution. A multilevel layout can combine distribution and range requirements. More partitions also create administrative and query overhead, so a high partition count needs a clear purpose. [2]

For a large ACDOCA with period-driven reporting, I'd start by testing a range-based layout and checking whether the main queries actually prune partitions. Then I'd size the largest planned range before choosing its boundaries and the partition count.

Projected rows per range ≈ projected ACDOCA rows per period × periods in the range. Where volumes vary, sum the period-specific projections instead. Include existing rows and expected additions through the planning horizon, including late postings into older periods. Count physical ACDOCA rows across the relevant ledgers, rather than assuming one business journal line equals one row.

Compare the largest projected range with the operational threshold described below. If it approaches that threshold, test narrower ranges first. When even one period is too large, or finer ranges create excessive overhead, my next candidate is a multilevel layout that also uses hash distribution within each range. Column and key restrictions can require multilevel partitioning before capacity does. Check the current finance guidance in SAP Note 2289491 and partitioning FAQ 2044468 before choosing FISCYEARPER, BELNR, the level order or a single-level definition. [3] [4]

SAP documents a maximum of 2,147,483,648 rows per column-store partition for HANA 2.0 SPS 08. Set an operational threshold well below that boundary, based on growth and the time needed to complete another change. [5] SAP's administration training suggests up to 1.5 billion rows when addressing the row limit, with fewer where substantial growth is expected. That isn't a fixed target for every ACDOCA system. [2]

A range design needs an owner for future ranges and the OTHERS partition. Adding a range can move matching data out of OTHERS, which becomes expensive if it has accumulated many rows. [2] For other large tables, check application ownership of partition management as well: SAP BW, for example, manages its own partitioning. [1]

2. Reassess the existing partition layout

For an established system, first identify what's forcing the change. A fast-growing partition, uneven distribution, reporting latency and a difficult maintenance window lead to different tests. Compare the current and candidate layouts using representative data and workload, then choose how to carry out the change.

Route When it fits

Native offline repartitioningThe operation and its recovery allowance fit the measured capacity and business window.
Native online partitioningThe revision supports the required change, and rehearsal shows acceptable locking, temporary resource use and business response.
SLT with a prepared replacementMoving the copy ahead of cutover addresses the window constraint, and the application-specific switch is supported and rehearsed.

Start by testing the native route. If its resource demands, elapsed time and recovery allowance fit, there's a strong case for keeping the change within HANA's partitioning operation. If the copy work can't fit the window, evaluate an SLT rebuild with SAP and establish whether staging, change catch-up and reconciliation can run alongside business activity. Table size alone doesn't settle that choice.

Start with this read-only snapshot in the relevant tenant database. Replace YOUR_SCHEMA with the application schema and adapt the table filter for another column-store table. The queries require monitoring privileges and use HANA 2.0 SPS 08 view definitions. Memory values use GiB, calculated as bytes divided by 1,073,741,824. [6]

SELECT HOST, PORT, PART_ID, IS_REPLICA, LOADED, RECORD_COUNT,
       ROUND(MEMORY_SIZE_IN_TOTAL / 1073741824.0, 2) AS TOTAL_GIB,
       ROUND(MEMORY_SIZE_IN_DELTA / 1073741824.0, 2) AS DELTA_GIB
FROM SYS.M_CS_TABLES
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME = 'YOUR_SCHEMA'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'ACDOCA'
ORDER BY RECORD_COUNT DESC, HOST, PORT, PART_ID;

Read memory alongside LOADED, whose values are NO, PARTIALLY and FULL. A partition that is unloaded or only partly loaded can need more memory when additional columns are accessed; its current footprint doesn't tell you how many rows it holds. Keep host, port and replica status with each observation. Delta memory is already included in total memory, so don't add it again. [6] SAP also warns that some memory estimates can show zero after a split or merge until a delta merge updates them. Interpret those values with the operation's state. [7]

3. Size and rehearse the native SQL operation

Before estimating a change, establish what “table size” measures: persisted data, loaded table memory or another metric. Then measure what the proposed operation adds while the rest of the database is running. SAP documents memory-allocation failures during repartitioning and treats additional disk space as a separate question. [8] [9]

One check is easy to miss: the memory available to the host and the memory allowed to a statement are separate constraints. HANA can stop a statement when its applicable memory limit is reached. User settings and workload-class mappings need review alongside the HANA allocation limits, including the threshold that controls when a statement limit applies. [10] [11] Record the effective settings used in rehearsal and check the production execution context against them.

The rehearsal should cover the proposed layout at representative scale, including data skew and the competing workload. Record elapsed time, peak host and statement memory, CPU, data and log growth, and business response. Include abort and recovery time in the maintenance plan. A run that finishes just before the window closes leaves little room for an unexpected result.

Use SAP KBA 3215774 as a reference for monitoring and investigating a long-running repartitioning operation. [12] Native online partitioning can reduce lock duration, but the exact operation and revision still matter. SAP also documents an online-partitioning failure associated with a statement-memory limit during replica synchronization. [13] [14]

4. Move the copy ahead of cutover where SLT fits

An SLT-based design can prepare a partitioned replacement while the original continues serving the business. That leaves the final outage to cover remaining changes, reconciliation, the application-table switch and validation. The benefit has a capacity cost: both paths have to run together during the copy.

For an application-owned table such as ACDOCA, establish the supported switch and recovery procedure with SAP for the relevant release. Include ABAP Dictionary consistency, indexes, dependencies and downstream consumers. Replication documentation on its own doesn't establish that an application table can be replaced with a replica.

Check target creation and refresh behavior before loading. In Advanced Replication Settings (transaction LTRS), a partition command can be supplied for table creation, while refresh options can recreate a prepared target. SAP also describes S/4HANA scenarios in which Alternative Table Name is unavailable. Validate the actual mapping and target behavior in the proposed configuration. [15]

Figure 1. Conceptual reading-type-5 example showing the original, replacement and applicable staging store. A supported application-table switch and recovery procedure are prerequisites.

5. Plan for memory, disk and processing capacity

During a staged rebuild, the live table, growing replacement and any resident staging data may share the same HANA host. Extraction and inserts also need working memory. Merges add another overlap: SAP describes the original main storage remaining available while a new main is built and new changes enter a second delta. Size the affected partitions and concurrent merges, rather than assuming a fixed multiplier for the whole database. [16]

Build separate disk and memory budgets

Collect synchronized measurements through loading, catch-up and recovery. Start from the normal host baseline, identify the additional allocations, and compare the combined observations with service and host totals. Count the live table once. Keep persisted staging bytes separate from staging memory, and use consistent decimal TB or binary TiB units.

Resource Evidence to collect

Table persistenceSource, replacement and staging disk bytes, their locations and how long they coexist.
Resident table memoryLoaded source, replacement and staging memory; main and delta counted once.
Additional working memoryChange queues, extraction and load buffers, and merge or compression allocations outside the table totals.
Storage capacityUsed and allocated data volumes, log growth, free filesystem space and recovery requirements.
Processing and business responseCPU, I/O latency, sustained throughput, replication lag and transaction response times.

Here is a separate persistence query. Its disk bytes describe table data at each listed location; filesystem consumption also includes allocated volume space, logs and other files. [17]

SELECT HOST, PORT, PART_ID,
       ROUND(DISK_SIZE / 1073741824.0, 2) AS DISK_GIB
FROM SYS.M_TABLE_PERSISTENCE_LOCATION_STATISTICS
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME = 'YOUR_SCHEMA'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'ACDOCA'
ORDER BY DISK_SIZE DESC, HOST, PORT, PART_ID;

At the busiest point, compare source, replacement, staging and working allocations that actually coexist. Adding each component's highest value from a different time can overstate simultaneous consumption. Reserve further capacity for workload variation and recovery, then check the effective HANA limits and physical host capacity, allowing separately for the operating system. Remote source, target and SLT hosts need their own budgets.

Measure throughput alongside resource use

More parallel jobs help only while useful throughput improves and business response remains acceptable. Reading, serialization, inserts, compression and merges consume resources at different points in the run. SAP's merge-token mechanism ties merge scheduling to available resources. [18]

For a hypothetical initial load of 12 billion rows, a sustained rate of 100,000 rows per second gives 33.3 hours: 12 billion ÷ 100,000 ÷ 3,600. At 50,000 rows per second, the same arithmetic gives 66.7 hours. These illustrative rates exclude setup, change catch-up, reconciliation and cutover; use measured throughput for the actual plan.

A 24-hour query filter won't cover a load that runs for several days. For a multi-day rehearsal, use _SYS_STATISTICS.HOST_DELTA_MERGE_STATISTICS; the example below looks back seven days. SAP HANA 2.0 SPS 08 documents 42 days of history with a 300-second collection interval. Check collection and retention before the run so the history covers the whole exercise. [19]

SELECT SNAPSHOT_ID, HOST, PORT, PART_ID, START_TIME,
       TYPE, MOTIVATION,
       ROUND(EXECUTION_TIME / 1000.0, 2) AS DURATION_SECONDS,
       SUCCESS, LAST_ERROR, ERROR_DESCRIPTION
FROM _SYS_STATISTICS.HOST_DELTA_MERGE_STATISTICS
WHERE SCHEMA_NAME = 'YOUR_SCHEMA'
  AND TABLE_NAME = 'ACDOCA'
  AND TYPE IN ('MERGE', 'SPARSE')
  AND START_TIME >= ADD_DAYS(CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, -7)
ORDER BY START_TIME DESC, HOST, PORT, PART_ID, SNAPSHOT_ID;

The filter includes delta merges and compression optimization, excluding hint records whose status has a different meaning. An unsuccessful call needs its error description: a call can decide that no merge is necessary. For recent activity, SYS.M_DELTA_MERGE_STATISTICS remains useful before the next history collection. [20] START_TIME is the operation's start time; SNAPSHOT_ID is the UTC collection timestamp. Align timestamps with host and service telemetry when investigating peaks, and don't count repeated observations of one operation as separate merges. [19]

6. Watch staging growth during the initial load

Track sender staging and the replacement table separately during the initial load. A queue can keep growing while the target is still loading, adding pressure to the host even when extraction looks healthy. Compare queue growth, target throughput, replication lag and business response on the same timeline before increasing concurrency.

The SAP SLT Performance Optimization Guide, document version 2.2 dated 2025-10-08, identifies DMC_INDXCL for legacy sender-queue reading types 4/5 and DHCDC_RTSTORE for subscription-based reading type 5. It describes staging growth during initial load and deletion after completion. The guide's pooled- and cluster-table space estimates are not an ACDOCA sizing rule. [21]

The staging-store name changed between guide versions. The 2021 guide names DMC_INDXCL in its subscription-based section; the 2025 guide uses DHCDC_RTSTORE there. Match observations to the component versions and recording mechanism. [22] [21]

Figure 2. Conceptual reading-type-5 lifecycle with separate qualitative scales. The curves show no production measurements or sizing ratio, and queue cleanup does not predict when allocated data-volume files shrink.

The 2025 guide also describes subscription-based reading type 1, which avoids intermediate payload staging in DHCDC_RTSTORE, subject to prerequisites and a transfer-time trade-off. Test the eligible reading methods for your components. [21] After an interruption, follow the cleanup or restart procedure for that method: SAP documents initial-load errors after DMC_INDXCL entries are removed. [23]

Deleting staging records and reclaiming physical disk space are separate events. Check both used and allocated data-volume space and the revision's reclaim behavior. Include that distinction in the recovery plan so cleanup isn't mistaken for immediately available filesystem capacity. [24]

7. Reconcile before reopening the business

Begin reconciliation during rehearsal and leave time to investigate differences, correct them and repeat the comparison. A matching total count can still conceal missing, extra or differing records. Define key-level comparisons and business totals, including the treatment of deletes, archiving and any filters. SAP's Cross-Database Comparison integration provides a useful reference for data-level comparison. [25]

Monitor outstanding changes, their age and replication latency as the cutover approaches. [26] A finished initial load is one milestone; the decision to proceed also depends on consistent data, a manageable backlog and time to complete the application checks.

During the cutover window, stop business writers and drain active transactions while keeping the runtime required to apply final changes available. Complete the consistency checks and rehearsed switch sequence, validate application access and downstream behavior, then reopen. Set a go/no-go deadline that preserves time for recovery and confirm the required backup and recovery prerequisites before starting.

A retained original table needs particular care. Once postings resume against the replacement, the retained copy becomes stale. Recovery must account for those new transactions; renaming the old table back can't, by itself, restore a consistent current state.

Conclusion

Start the next partition change while there's still time to test it. Whether the table is ACDOCA or another large business table, choose a route that rehearsal shows can complete the cutover, or recover if needed, within the business window. Which constraint is boxing you in right now: partition growth, memory headroom, replication catch-up or the window?

Tell me in the comments, or send me a message about the trade-off you're working through.

SAP references

References checked October 2026. The technical scope is SAP HANA Platform 2.0, including SPS 08, and SLT. entry.title: Your AI agents are only as good as the knowledge behind them
entry.content:
Enterprises are deploying AI agents faster than they can teach them how the business actually works.

An agent assigned to approve a purchase order, screen a customer, or close the books doesn't fail because the model isn't capable. It fails because it doesn't know your rules: the approval threshold for EMEA orders above €100k, the exception that requires board sign-off, the compliance step that is never optional. That knowledge rarely lives anywhere an agent can reach it. It is scattered across 500-page policy documents, SharePoint sites, Confluence pages, email threads, and the heads of the three people who have been there long enough to remember why the rule exists.

So teams do the only thing they can: they hand-curate a bundle of documents and paste it into each agent's prompt. It works for a demo. Then a rule changes, the bundle goes stale, two departments encode the same policy differently, and nobody discovers the drift until an audit does. Every new agent starts the same context-gathering from scratch. The promise of the agentic enterprise stalls, not on the agents, but on the fractured, static knowledge underneath them.

This is the gap SAP Company Memory preview is built to close.

A governed knowledge layer, not another document store

SAP Company Memory is a governed knowledge layer that delivers an organization's business rules, policies, and institutional knowledge to AI agents and to people at the moment of decision.

The difference from a wiki or knowledge base is structural. Instead of storing documents and hoping consumers can find the right passage, SAP Company Memory turns scattered rules into atoms: small, consistent, retrievable units. Each atom carries three things:

  • Purpose: why the rule exists
  • Scope: when it applies (region, role, process, system)
  • Rule: the exact governing statement

Every atom keeps a citation back to its source document and page, so any answer can be traced to its origin. Atoms carry hierarchy too. A global sanctions rule, a company-wide policy, a regional exception, a customer-specific term can all coexist, and the right one surfaces for the right context, the way a well-briefed employee would apply it.

Because the knowledge is structured once and governed centrally, it can be consumed many ways:

  • Agents connect at runtime over MCP and retrieve exactly the rules relevant to the decision in front of them, with no manual SOP-to-prompt translation and no vendor lock-in.
  • Developers query and export structured rule sets through a CLI at build time.
  • People ask questions in plain language and get a specific, cited answer back.

And when rules collide, for example "orders below €20 need approval" in one document and "orders below €20 don't" in another, SAP Company Memory scans the whole corpus, surfaces the conflict, and walks an owner through resolving it before any agent ever consumes a contradiction.

The same layer that governs agents answers your people's questions too

Here is the part that surprises teams: the knowledge you structure to make agents reliable turns out to be exactly what your people have been missing.

The rules buried in that 500-page document weren't only invisible to agents. They were invisible to the new hire on day three, to the process owner trying to work out what breaks if a policy changes, to the employee who asks a colleague and still gets it wrong. Make the knowledge explicit, governed, and queryable, and the human side lights up:

  • Instant, cited answers to policy questions. "What's our approval threshold for EMEA orders above €100k?" returns a specific atom with its source, not a link to a PDF to go read.
  • Onboarding in days, not months. New hires query SAP Company Memory instead of shadowing colleagues to absorb tribal knowledge.
  • Impact analysis before a change. "What breaks if we change this rule?" is answered in seconds, not weeks of manual cross-referencing.
  • Authoring by the people who own the rules. Business owners write and maintain rules in natural language, rather than filing a ticket with a technical team.
  • Knowledge that survives people leaving. Institutional memory becomes explicit and retrievable instead of walking out the door.

The two audiences reinforce each other. Humans author and validate the rules; agents consume them at runtime; what we learn from execution feeds back to the people maintaining them. The knowledge layer gets more valuable the more it is used.

The foundation is already in place

A business-rules layer for agents is only as good as the rules that feed it. The hard part is not building the retrieval layer; it is cold-starting a corpus of real, validated enterprise rules that agents can actually rely on.

SAP enters this with a foundation already assembled:

  • Process models that specify how a business should run, built from two decades of enterprise process design in SAP Signavio.
  • Execution data from business process intelligence and S/4HANA that shows how it actually runs, so rules can be grounded in reality, not just asserted.
  • Domain expertise packaged across thousands of SAP reference models and content packages.
  • The business owners themselves, already working inside the tools where this knowledge lives.

Where we are, and where we're headed

SAP Company Memory is in the hands of selected design partners today, through an early-access program running on SAP Signavio infrastructure. We are deliberately building this with customers rather than announcing it finished; the beta partners are shaping ingestion, governance, and the human query experience as we go.

Broader availability follows as that validation matures. We will share specifics on timing as we get closer; for now, the direction is clear and the foundation is in customers' hands.

What we are building toward is a self-enriching organizational memory: a knowledge layer that humans trust for answers, agents rely on to execute correctly, and systems draw on for consistency, one that gets sharper every time it is used.

If your organization is deploying AI agents into business processes and running into the knowledge gap described here, we'd like to talk. We're expanding the design-partner program and are especially interested in teams working through agent governance, onboarding, and compliance.

Want to know more? Feel free to reach out!

entry.title: Re: How to restrict cross-creation between Customers and...
entry.content:
Authorization object B_BUPA_RLT only controls which BP Roles a user can maintain (such as FLVN00/FLVN01 for vendors or FLCU00/FLCU01 for customers).

However, when a BP is created using a specific Grouping, the CVI framework can automatically create corresponding Customer or Vendor master records in the background based on:

  • BP Grouping ↔ Customer Account Group mapping
  • BP Grouping ↔ Vendor Account Group mapping
  • CVI synchronization settings

As a result:

  • User creates BP with a "Vendor" role.
  • Selected grouping is mapped to both Vendor and Customer account groups.
  • CVI creates Customer data automatically.
  • B_BUPA_RLT does not prevent this because the user is not explicitly maintaining the Customer BP role.

To achieve strict segregation between Vendor and Customer creation in BP:

1) Use separate BP Groupings

  • Vendor grouping (e.g., ZVEN) mapped only to Vendor Account Groups.
  • Customer grouping (e.g., ZCUS) mapped only to Customer Account Groups.

2) Restrict BP Roles

  • Vendor users: FLVN00, FLVN01
  • Customer users: FLCU00, FLCU01
  • Control via authorization object B_BUPA_RLT.

3) Restrict Account Groups

  • Vendor users: authorize only F_LFA1_GRP.
  • Customer users: authorize only F_KNA1_GRP.

4) Optional Enhancement

  • Implement a BP validation BAdI/User Exit to prevent users from selecting unauthorized BP Groupings.

entry.title: From blind spot to threat signal: feed SAP Application Vulnerability Report into Microsoft Sentinel
entry.content:
co-authored by Martin Pankraz

Dear community, 

Since April 2026, your custom BAIP apps have officially graduated: they are now first-class targets for the hacker community in software supply chain attacks. The customers who ran vulnerability scanning at the time spotted the exposure fastest and rolled out SAP's fixes within hours. Everyone else found out the hard way. According to Microsoft’s latest digital defense report 2026: “Open-source supply chain compromise” is the number one emerging threat for the next year (see page 36, threat landscape). 

Knowing which CVE sits in your custom app on BAIP is only half the job. You also need to know whether someone is actively exploiting it right now - and that signal lives in your SOC, not in a scan report. 

A mental model to dissect this space 

  • Shift Left - secure code before it ships (static analysis, dependency scanning in your pipeline). 
  • Shield Right - protect and monitor the running app at runtime. 
  • The missing link - take the application vulnerability report's runtime findings and correlate them everything else happening across your estate using your SIEM application. 

This article is about that third piece. The application vulnerability report tells you a known CVE is live in a BAIP custom app. Microsoft Sentinel for SAP tells you the same tenant just saw a suspicious Entra ID sign-in, lateral movement, and sensitive SAP data download. Alone, each is noise. Together, they are an incident! See below incident graph and timeline informed by Microsoft Sentinel for SAP on the Microsoft Defender portal from an SAP attack replay. 

 

What the application vulnerability report gives you 

SAP's first-party application vulnerability report continuously identifies known CVEs in the custom applications you run on BAIP - no agent to deploy, no separate scanner to license. It is the authoritative, SAP-sourced view of what is vulnerable in your code. If you are new to the Application Vulnerability Report, this is the fastest way to see your BAIP custom-code exposure. 

Bringing it into Microsoft Sentinel for SAP BAIP 

With the integration of the application vulnerability report into the Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP BAIP, your existing BAIP telemetry is enriched with these CVE findings. See below Screenshot from the Microsoft Sentinel Incident overview on the correlation of the SAP BAIP audit log and the Application Vulnerability Report findings. 

It features the vulnerable CAP app which was used during the red team event at DSAG TechXChange 2026 showing AI prompt injection attacks. 

 

The vulnerability signal can now be correlated with the rest of your security data. 

Beyond the automatic correlation, you get out-of-the-box visualizations for querying and continuous monitoring, built for the people who own BAIP security day to day. If you already run the application vulnerability report but have never pushed its findings into a SIEM, this is the step that turns a periodic report into a live detection surface. See below visuals produced from the API output of the new vulnerability report service. 

A mesh of screenshots from the updated workbook on Microsoft Sentinel for SAP 

Comparing with shift-left approaches 

GitHub Advanced Security is one sample of tackling vulnerabilities with the shift-left approach during design time till your DevOps pipelines and before code is put into production. It is excellent at what it does: finding vulnerabilities in source code before it ever ships. It scans your repositories, flags vulnerable dependencies, and catches secrets in commits. 

The application vulnerability report answers a different question. It does not look at your repository; it looks at what is running on BTP and tells you which known CVEs are live in production right now. 

GitHub Advanced Security secures the code on its way in. The application vulnerability report, correlated in Sentinel, tells you whether a live vulnerability is being exploited. They are complementary: one hardens the pipeline, the other watches the runtime. 

What's next? 

We are expanding the correlation content: more out-of-the-box detection rules mapping application vulnerability report findings to active-exploitation signals, and richer workbooks for BAIP security personas. Expect tighter mapping between specific CVE classes and attacker behaviors that typically follow them. 

In addition to that we would like to hear from you what you need most from the BAIP vulnerability space. 

Get started today  

  1. Enable the application vulnerability report for your BAIP custom apps. 
  2. Deploy the latest Microsoft Sentinel Solution for SAP BAIP v 3.2.1. 
  3. Turn on the application vulnerability report connector (preview*) using the service key, so CVE findings flow into Sentinel for SAP BTP. 
  4. Deploy the workbook “BAIP Activity” and analytic rules shipped with the Sentinel solution for SAP BAIP 
  5. Discover your current vulnerable apps from the workbook, and watch for correlated incidents, where a known vulnerability meets suspicious runtime activity. 

Shift Left secures the code. Shield Right protects the runtime. Correlating the application vulnerability report in your SIEM closes the loop between the two. 

* the connector remains in preview while the Application Vulnerability Report service is in Beta. 

Closing the loop 

Custom applications on SAP BAIP need continuous vulnerability visibility - but isolated findings are only the beginning. By bringing SAP application vulnerability report findings into Microsoft Sentinel, your SOC can connect known CVEs in production with suspicious activity across the broader environment and investigate incidents with the context they need. 

Shift Left and Shield Right serve different, complementary purposes: solutions such as GitHub Advanced Security help secure code throughout development and delivery, while the SAP application vulnerability report identifies known vulnerabilities in applications already running on BAIP. Correlating those runtime findings in Sentinel closes the gap between vulnerable code and active threats. 

Through close collaboration between SAP and Microsoft engineering, Microsoft Sentinel for SAP BAIP now delivers a broader, more actionable view of application risk. 

Now we want to hear from you: which detections, analytics rules, or workbook insights would make the biggest difference for your SAP BAIP security operations? Share your priorities in the comments or reach out to us directly. 

Cheers 

Fabian and Martin

entry.title: I Built an AI Data Assistant for My PM Team Inside SAP
entry.content:
Here's What Modern PM Work Looks Like 

A significant chunk of my week used to look like this.

Open SAP's internal cloud reporting system, filter by industry, export the table. Open SAC, find the right story, apply the filter again. Switch to the CSAT tab, reconcile customer names that never quite match across systems. Then finally answer the question a colleague asked 45 minutes ago.

It wasn't broken. But it wasn't good enough for the pace we need to move at.

So I built something.

 

What I Built

The Industries PM AI Assistant is a natural-language interface over six live SAP data sources. Any PM on our team can ask a question in plain English and get a synthesized answer in under a minute.

Instead of navigating dashboards, you type:

"Show me deal qualification data for Chemicals. What are the top redirect reasons, and do we have CSAT feedback from those customers?"

The assistant pulls redirect counts, ranks the reasons, surfaces relevant satisfaction feedback, and connects the narrative. It runs as a live web app on SAP BTP.

Data sources it talks to:

  • SAP's internal cloud reporting system: customer adoption, scope item usage, instance counts
  • SAC Analytics Cloud: Deal qualification data (17,000+ rows) via the SAP Analytics Cloud API
  • CSAT / Qualtrics: customer satisfaction feedback, enriched with industry via customer master join
  • Competitive battlecards: market intelligence, on demand

It runs on Claude via SAP BTP AI services. No data leaves SAP infrastructure.

 

Why This Matters

Our team covers 12+ industry verticals. Every week we're trying to answer questions like:

  • Which industries have the highest redirect rates, and why?
  • What are Chemicals customers saying in CSAT?
  • Which scope items have low adoption in Process Industries?
  • Where are we losing deals, and to whom?

Each of those requires pulling from two or three systems that don't share a customer ID, don't use the same industry taxonomy, and certainly don't talk to each other.

The assistant does the joining, the filtering, and the synthesis. The PM just asks.

 

The Part That Surprised Me Most

The most impressive capability isn't the data retrieval. It's the cross-source reasoning.

Real example from testing. I asked:

"Show me CSAT for Chemicals customers."

The problem: CSAT has no industry field. There is no Chemicals column to filter on.

Here's what the assistant did:

  • Flagged the limitation: CSAT rows have no industry tag
  • Proposed a fix: name-match CSAT respondents against the Chemicals deal qualification data customer list
  • Ran a fuzzy join across both datasets despite naming differences
  • When the direct join was thin, used the L3-Area field as a manufacturing proxy to surface more relevant feedback
  • Connected the CSAT complaints to the redirect reasons from earlier in the conversation

That kind of analysis used to take a data analyst an afternoon. The assistant did it in a single query, mid-conversation.

 

What This Looks Like Day to Day

Before: I need redirect data for Chemicals for the QBR. Let me pull the SAC story, filter by industry, export, then cross with CSAT...

After: "Summarize redirect trends for Chemicals and flag any CSAT signals." Done in one query.

Before: Which scope items should I prioritize for Process Industries? Let me check CDO, filter by industry, sort by usage rate...

After: "Which scope items have the lowest activation rate in Process Industries?" Instant answer with a chart.

Before: Spending the first 30 minutes of a customer prep call pulling data.

After: Ask the assistant to brief you. Spend those 30 minutes on strategy instead.

 

The Honest Build Story

This was built by a PM. Not a developer, not a data engineer. A PM with some technical background, an AI coding assistant, and evenings.

The stack:

  • Python and FastAPI backend
  • Playwright for browser automation on JS-rendered SAP data sources
  • SAC SAP Analytics Cloud API: SAP Analytics Cloud's API, which bypasses UI pagination and returns the full dataset server-side
  • Claude API via SAP BTP AI services
  • SAP BTP Cloud Foundry for always-on deployment

The hardest part wasn't the AI. It was the data plumbing. Authentication, session management, hidden pagination in SAP's internal cloud reporting system, JS-rendered tables in SAC. That took the majority of build time.

But it's solved. The app re-authenticates automatically, handles session expiry, detects VPN state, and degrades gracefully when a source is unavailable.

 

What's Next

The current version fetches live data from SAP's internal cloud reporting system and SAC. In December 2026, we're migrating the data layer to SAP Data Products. That means cleaner APIs, better governance, and a more scalable foundation that other teams can replicate.

On the roadmap:

  • Automated weekly PM briefings, generated without any manual trigger
  • Jira integration to surface open influence requests and sprint items in context
  • More data sources as SAP's data product catalog grows

 

Why I'm Writing This

Not to show off a tool.

The point is what it represents. PM work looks different when you treat AI as infrastructure rather than a shortcut. The time that used to go into pulling and reconciling data now goes into analysis, customer conversations, and roadmap decisions.

And the bar to build something like this, for a PM with technical curiosity and the right tools, is lower than most people think.

 

Get Involved

If you're a PM in SAP, the assistant is live on BTP. Reach out and I'll get you access or we can talk of extending the app with the data you need.

If you're building something similar inside SAP, happy to share the approach and what I'd do differently. Drop a comment or connect with me directly.

 

Akshay Kaore is a Product Manager for SAP S/4HANA Cloud ERP Industries, focused on Process Industries and Chemicals. 12 years at SAP across engineering, DevOps, and product. He runs AI enablement for the Industries PM team. This post is part of the AI Product Management series on SAP Community. The views expressed here are my own and do not represent the position of my employer.

entry.title: Unlocking Commerce Intelligence: A Practitioner's Guide to SAP CX AI Toolkit for SAP Commerce Cloud
entry.content:
Introduction: Why AI in Commerce Is No Longer Optional

The commerce landscape has fundamentally shifted. Customers expect instant, personalized, and accurate product experiences — at every touchpoint, at scale. Managing thousands of product listings, keeping content fresh, delivering intelligent search, and responding to customer questions in real time are challenges that no team can sustainably address through manual effort alone.

SAP CX AI Toolkit is SAP's answer to this challenge. But it is more than a collection of useful AI features — it is the execution layer of SAP's Autonomous Unified Commerce and Customer Experience vision: an AI-powered platform that connects marketing, commerce, sales, and service into a single autonomous system, where AI acts on the live operational truth of the business.

Understanding this connection is important for every practitioner evaluating or implementing the toolkit. The tools and agents you configure today are not isolated capabilities — they are the concrete, deployable components of a strategic architecture designed to make commerce experiences continuously connected, trusted, and autonomous.

This blog post covers the full spectrum of AI tools available to SAP Commerce Cloud practitioners, from content generation and image creation to intelligent customer engagement, marketing automation, custom tool building, AI agents, and the emerging frontier of autonomous commerce. Before diving into the individual tools, the following section establishes the strategic and architectural context that makes the toolkit's design choices meaningful.

SAP CX AI Toolkit Web App Home Page — showing the left navigation menu with AI Tools, AI Agents, Product Images, Visual Search, and AI Tools Builder highlighted.

Part 0: The Bigger Picture — CX AI Toolkit and Autonomous Unified Commerce

0.1 What Is Autonomous Unified Commerce?

SAP's Autonomous Unified Commerce — part of Autonomous CX — is a strategic vision and platform architecture in which AI connects and orchestrates the full Lead-to-Cash process across marketing, commerce, sales, and service as one coordinated system. Rather than AI functioning as a set of add-on features within individual applications, Autonomous Unified Commerce positions AI as the operating layer of the entire customer-facing enterprise: intent-driven, outcome-oriented, and grounded in the live data that powers every business process.

The vision for SAP Commerce Cloud within this architecture is explicit: "Enable every enterprise to continuously deliver connected, trusted, and autonomous commerce experiences that drive profitable growth and optimal customer outcomes."

The SAP CX AI Toolkit is the vehicle through which this vision becomes operational. It is not a roadmap item — it is available to configure, deploy, and measure in production today.

0.2 Where the Toolkit Fits: The Agentic Application Layer

SAP envisions AI agents evolving through three levels of autonomy as part of what it calls the Autonomous Enterprise — a model where business processes are intent-driven, execute across application boundaries, and keep humans informed and in control at critical decision points. The CX AI Toolkit's agents and tools operate inside this agentic application layer: not as isolated utilities, but as interconnected components of one system spanning SAP Commerce Cloud, SAP Sales Cloud, SAP Service Cloud, and the SAP Customer Data Platform.

This architectural positioning has a direct practical consequence: the same AI agents that enrich your product catalog are connected to the same data layer that drives your storefront search, your post-purchase service interactions, and your marketing personalization. The toolkit is designed to be one system, not many.

0.3 Five Integration Points That Connect the Toolkit to the Autonomous Commerce Vision

Understanding how the toolkit relates to the broader vision is easier when viewed through five concrete integration points:

  1. Agents as the Autonomous Commerce Engine The three Commerce AI agents within the toolkit — the Catalog Optimization Agent, the Shopping Agent, and the Digital Service Agent — together represent the practical implementation of autonomous commerce across the full customer lifecycle. The Shopping Agent transforms the storefront into a conversational sales associate. The Digital Service Agent extends autonomous support post-purchase. The Catalog Optimization Agent continuously audits and improves product data quality. Together they span pre-purchase discovery, conversion, and post-purchase service — the complete arc of customer experience.
  2. Grounded in Live Enterprise Data Autonomous Unified Commerce requires AI to act on the "full truth of the business." The SAP CX AI Toolkit connects directly to SAP Commerce Cloud product catalogs, customer data, and order history — and when integrated with the Cloud ERP— to real-time inventory, pricing, and order status from the backend. SAP CX AI Toolkit agents work with a synchronized product catalog from SAP Commerce Cloud, while pricing, stock availability, and order status are accessed in real-time directly from SAP Commerce Cloud. This is what makes autonomous execution reliable rather than brittle.
  3. Governed by SAP Business AI Security and Compliance Both the Autonomous CX platform and the CX AI Toolkit are anchored in SAP Business AI security, governance, and compliance — including zero data retention, PII obfuscation, and bias prevention. This Trusted AI Layer ensures that autonomous execution remains enterprise-grade. As AI agents take on more consequential actions — publishing content, responding to customers, modifying catalog data — governance is not optional. It is architecturally embedded.
  4. Cross-Portfolio Unification The toolkit connects natively to SAP Sales Cloud, SAP Service Cloud, SAP Commerce Cloud, and the SAP Customer Data Platform. This native connectivity is what enables AI to orchestrate workflows across the full Lead-to-Cash process — not just within Commerce, but across the entire customer-facing portfolio. A single customer interaction can draw on data from, and trigger actions in, multiple systems simultaneously.
  5. Human-in-the-Loop by Design Autonomous does not mean unsupervised. The CX AI Toolkit's agents are designed with human oversight built in at every meaningful decision point. Outputs can be reviewed before publishing, agent actions can be scoped and constrained, and confidence thresholds determine when the system escalates to a human. This design principle reflects the Autonomous Enterprise model's core commitment: AI augments human judgment; it does not replace it.

0.4 What This Means for Practitioners

For practitioners, this context reframes how to think about every tool in the toolkit. A product description generated by the Product Descriptions tool is not just a piece of content — it is a contribution to the catalog data layer that the Catalog Optimization Agent monitors, the Shopping Agent retrieves in real time during a customer conversation, and the Digital Service Agent references when answering a post-purchase question. Every tool feeds the same system.

This is why setup — tenant mapping, catalog configuration, authentication, and data source integration — matters so much. Getting the foundational integration right is not a technical prerequisite to check off; it is the act of connecting your Commerce Cloud environment to the autonomous commerce architecture. The sections that follow take you through every tool with this system-level perspective in mind.

Prerequisites: Getting Started

Before diving into the tools themselves, it is important to establish the foundational setup. All AI tools discussed in this blog require an active SAP Commerce Cloud license, and access is controlled at the tenant level within SAP CX AI Toolkit.

The initial setup involves three key steps:

Step 1 — Tenant Mapping: Your SAP CX AI Toolkit tenant must be mapped to your SAP Commerce Cloud tenant. This mapping is what allows the toolkit to access your product catalog, retrieve product data, and push generated content back to Commerce.

Step 2 — Catalog and Classification Setup: The classification ID and catalog ID from your SAP Commerce Cloud instance must be added to the SAP CX AI Toolkit configuration. This ensures the AI tools are pointing at the correct product data structures.

Step 3 — Credentials and Authentication: Your SAP Commerce Cloud OAuth credentials must be configured within SAP CX AI Toolkit. Additionally, product images that are sourced from SAP Commerce Cloud must be publicly accessible via URL, and the relevant IP addresses must be whitelisted.

Once this integration is established, you can access the full suite of Commerce AI tools through the SAP CX AI Toolkit Web App, Chrome Extension (Joule), or the embedded panel — depending on your team's workflow preferences.

Settings / Commerce / User Configuration page in SAP CX AI Toolkit showing an active SAP Commerce Cloud product and classification catalog connection.

Part 1: AI-Powered Product Content

1.1 Product Attributes

Managing product attributes at scale is one of the most time-intensive tasks in any commerce operation. Inconsistent attribute data leads to poor search relevance, failed filters, and ultimately lower conversion rates. The Product Attributes tool addresses this by using AI to generate new attributes and attribute values for existing items and objects within your catalog. It also enables translation of attribute values directly from the screen, supporting multilingual catalog management without manual intervention.

Think of this tool as an intelligent data enrichment engine. Rather than manually tagging hundreds of SKUs with color, material, dimensions, or technical specifications, the AI analyzes your product data and generates contextually accurate attribute values. This not only accelerates catalog onboarding for new products but also helps standardize attribute quality across existing catalog items — a critical foundation for downstream capabilities like faceted search and personalized recommendations.

In the context of Autonomous Unified Commerce, high-quality, consistent attribute data is not just operationally valuable — it is the raw material that AI agents consume. The Catalog Optimization Agent depends on well-structured attributes to identify gaps and inconsistencies at scale, and the Shopping Agent draws on attribute data to answer customer questions accurately in real time. Every attribute enriched here improves the intelligence of the entire system.

Product Attributes tool screen showing a product selected, with AI-generated attribute names and values.

1.2 Product Descriptions

Product descriptions are arguably the most impactful piece of content on any product detail page. They influence SEO, customer decision-making, and brand perception. The Product Descriptions tool enables teams to generate rich, personalized product descriptions using generative AI that is grounded in your actual catalog data.

What makes this tool particularly powerful in practice is its support for prompt templates, which allow merchandising and content teams to define the style, audience, and tone of every description. For example, the documents include practical template patterns such as:

  • A luxury brand template that instructs the AI to write refined, sophisticated descriptions using elegant language that evokes exclusivity and premium craftsmanship, targeting a 150-word output.
  • An eco-friendly brand template that emphasizes sustainability, ethical sourcing, and environmental responsibility, with warm and inviting language for eco-conscious consumers at around 200 words.
  • A mountaineering product template that targets professional outdoor enthusiasts with a professional and rugged tone focused on reliability, durability, and performance at 125 words.

These templates illustrate an important design principle: the AI is only as good as the prompt you give it. Investing time upfront in defining your brand voice and description standards directly translates into higher-quality AI outputs that require minimal human editing. The tool also supports bulk description generation, allowing teams to process multiple products at once, review the output, and publish directly to SAP Commerce Cloud — significantly accelerating catalog enrichment projects.

Product Descriptions tool showing template dropdown, tone selector, length options, and a generated description for a sample product alongside its catalog attributes.

Part 2: Visual Commerce

2.1 Product Image Generation and Enhancement

High-quality product imagery is a commercial necessity, but traditional photography is expensive, slow, and difficult to scale — especially during rapid catalog expansion or seasonal campaigns. The Product Images tool integrates AI-driven image generation and editing directly into your Commerce workflow, offering a cost-effective alternative that does not compromise visual quality.

The tool operates in several modes:

Generate a New Image: You select a product from your catalog and provide a prompt — either by writing one manually, using AI-suggested prompts based on your product attributes, or using a combination of both. The AI generates a professional product image based on your instructions and the product's existing data.

Enhance an Existing Image: For products that already have images but where quality or presentation needs improvement, the enhancement capability allows you to refine those images without a full reshoot.

Add Image Overlays: You can add visual overlays to existing product images — for example, adding promotional badges, seasonal graphics, or brand elements directly onto catalog images.

Edit Objects in an Image: Object-level editing allows granular modifications within an existing product image, such as changing background environments, adjusting product elements, or removing unwanted artifacts.

One practical implementation note worth highlighting: the prompt for image generation supports 22 languages, including English, German, French, Japanese, Spanish, Portuguese, and more. This means global commerce teams can write their image generation prompts in their native language, reducing friction and improving adoption.

Product Images tool showing the "Generate New Image" workflow — product selected on the left, image editing tools in the center, and generated image output on the right.

2.2 Visual Search

Visual Search fundamentally changes how customers discover products. Instead of typing a search query, a customer uploads an image — a photo from a magazine, a screenshot from social media, or a picture they took themselves — and the system finds matching or visually similar products from your catalog.

The Visual Search tool within SAP CX AI Toolkit is designed to be integrated directly into your storefront experience. It comes with two key intelligence features that go beyond simple image matching:

Object Detection: When enabled, the system analyzes the uploaded image, identifies individual objects within it, and numbers them. The user can then select a specific object within the image to search for — for example, if a customer uploads a lifestyle photo of a living room, they can select just the lamp, or just the chair, and search for that specific item in your catalog. This makes visual search practical even for complex, multi-object images.

Visual Information Extraction: This feature goes a step further by extracting structured information from the image itself. You can provide specific extraction instructions — for example, "only extract model numbers starting with RFG and ignore all other numbers and codes" — and the system will extract that data from the image. This is particularly useful in B2B or technical commerce scenarios where customers are searching by product specifications or part numbers captured in photographs.

The setup requires that product images in SAP Commerce Cloud are publicly accessible via URL, and the relevant IPs are whitelisted as part of the integration. The catalog and classification IDs must also be mapped correctly to ensure the visual search results are drawn from the right product catalog.

Visual Search tool showing an uploaded image on the left with numbered object detection overlays, and matching catalog products displayed on the right.

Part 3: Intelligent Customer Engagement

3.1 Ask About This Product

One of the most common friction points in online shopping is the gap between the information displayed on a product page and the specific question a customer has. This leads to abandoned carts, increased support requests, and lost conversions. The Ask About This Product tool addresses this directly by enabling natural language Q&A against your product catalog.

The tool uses natural language processing and document scanning technology to answer product-specific questions by analyzing a comprehensive range of product data sources:

  • Product descriptions and specifications from your Commerce catalog
  • Product attributes and classification data
  • Manuals, warranties, spec sheets, and other documents uploaded to the product in Commerce Backoffice
  • Product reviews

When a question is asked, the tool searches across all available sources and surfaces the answer under two separate tabs — Product Specifications and Product Reviews — clearly showing which source the answer was drawn from. This source transparency is a trust-building feature that serious commerce implementations should not overlook.

The supported document types for product-attached files are broad, covering .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, .csv, .pdf, .txt, .text, and .json, with a maximum file size of 100 MB per document. This gives content teams significant flexibility in how they structure and upload supporting product documentation.

Ask About This Product tool showing a product selected, a natural language question entered, and the answer displayed split across "Product Specifications" and "Product Reviews" tabs with source citations.

3.2 Summary of Product Reviews

Customer reviews are one of the most influential factors in purchase decisions, yet they are also one of the most time-consuming content types for shoppers to consume. A product with hundreds of reviews contains a wealth of signal — but most customers do not read beyond the first page. The Summary of Product Reviews tool solves this by generating a concise, AI-synthesized summary of all available reviews for a given product.

For commerce teams, this tool delivers value in two directions. First, it helps customers quickly understand the sentiment, strengths, and weaknesses of a product without reading every individual review — accelerating decision-making and improving the shopping experience. Second, it gives merchandising and product teams a fast way to audit review quality and identify products that may need attention based on recurring feedback patterns.

There are two prerequisites worth noting for implementation. First, the feature requires the "Allow processing of reviews" check to be explicitly enabled in the Commerce Organization Configuration under User Menu > Settings > Commerce Organization Configuration > Review Summary. Second, if you have an established integration that predates the current version of the toolkit, you may need to re-establish the integration to access this feature — or contact SAP support for guidance.

Summary of Product Reviews tool showing a product selected and an AI-generated summary of customer sentiment displayed below.

Part 4: AI-Driven Marketing Content

One of the most resource-intensive aspects of running a modern commerce platform is keeping marketing content fresh, consistent, and brand-aligned across every channel. SAP CX AI Toolkit provides three dedicated tools to automate this work: blog post generation, social media post creation, and product banner text generation.

4.1 Generate a Blog Post

Content marketing remains one of the highest-ROI channels for commerce — but producing high-quality, SEO-optimized blog content consistently is a challenge for most teams. The Generate a Blog Post tool allows content and marketing teams to produce product-specific blog posts directly from the SAP CX AI Toolkit, grounded in your actual product data.

The workflow is straightforward: you select a product by name or ID, provide a blog description (with a minimum of 40 characters to give the AI sufficient direction), add any special instructions, define the tone, and choose a length. The tool supports eight tone options — Professional, Happy, Empathetic, Casual, Witty, Personal, Direct, and Confident — covering the full range of brand voice styles that commerce teams work with.

For length, three options are available: Short (200–400 words), Medium (approximately 500 words), and Long (600–800 words). The generated post can be copied, edited, and published through your existing CMS workflow. Access requires an active SAP Commerce Cloud license.

Generate a Blog Post tool showing product selection, blog description and custom instructions input, tone selector set to "Professional", length set to "Medium", and a generated blog post output.

4.2 Create Social Media Posts

Managing a consistent social media presence across multiple platforms while keeping content product-relevant and on-brand is a significant operational overhead. The Create Social Media Posts tool streamlines this by generating platform-ready posts for X (Twitter), Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, all within SAP CX AI Toolkit.

The tool is designed with platform-specific brevity in mind. Length options are calibrated to social media norms: Short (fewer than 15 words), Medium (fewer than 25 words), and Long (fewer than 50 words). This makes the output immediately usable across channels without extensive editing.

Create Social Media Posts tool showing platform selector, product selection, custom instructions, and generated post output for Instagram.

Closing Thoughts: From Tools to Transformation

The individual capabilities described in this guide — attribute enrichment, description generation, visual search, review summarization, marketing content, and AI agents — are each valuable in their own right. But their full significance only becomes clear when viewed as components of the same system.

SAP CX AI Toolkit is the execution layer of Autonomous Unified Commerce. Every tool you configure contributes to a catalog data layer that AI agents consume in real time. Every agent you deploy is governed by the same Trusted AI Layer that makes autonomous execution enterprise-grade. Every integration you establish connects your Commerce Cloud environment to a cross-portfolio architecture spanning marketing, sales, service, and ERP.

For practitioners, this means the return on investment from the toolkit compounds over time. Better catalog data produces better agent responses. Better agent responses drive higher conversion and lower service costs. Lower service costs free up human teams to focus on the decisions that require judgment, creativity, and empathy — the things AI cannot and should not replace.

The vision is a commerce operation that is continuously self-improving: one where AI handles the repetitive, the data-intensive, and the always-on, while humans remain in the loop at every point that matters. This guide is your starting point.

entry.title: Integrating AI into the Order-to-Cash Process
entry.content:
Innovating Order-to-Cash Teaching with AI

    The Order-to-Cash (O2C) process in SAP S/4HANA represents one of the most important end-to-end business processes in an organization by cutting across multiple business functions—sales, marketing, supply chain, logistics, finance and customer service.  A typical O2C process can be represented as:

    Customer Inquiry → Quotation → Sales Order → Availability/ATP → Delivery → Picking & Packing → Goods Issue → Billing → Accounts Receivable → Payment

    With O2C process students need to understand why each activity is performed, how information flows across functions, how one decision affects subsequent activities, and how the process ultimately contributes to customer service and business performance.

    Students need to understand not only the individual steps but also questions such as:

    • Why is a quotation created before a sales order?
    • Is it necessary to create Inquiry and/or Quotation for creating Sales Order?
    • What information flows from the sales order to delivery?
    • What happens when sufficient inventory is not available?
    • Why does goods issue affect inventory and accounting?
    • How does billing create a financial transaction?
    • What happens to the customer's receivable after billing?
    • What business consequences arise when delivery is delayed?

    AI tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Copilot can be integrated at each of these learning points to enhance learning. AI can therefore be positioned as a learning companion around the SAP system, rather than as a replacement for SAP practice. Before entering the system, students can use ChatGPT to explore an Order-to-Cash business scenario, identify relevant process steps and formulate questions that they should investigate in SAP. During the exercise, they can use AI to explore alternative explanations for issues such as incomplete order confirmations, delivery delays, pricing discrepancies or blocked orders. After completing the SAP process, students can use AI to interpret the resulting information, analyse Order-to-Cash data, construct management summaries and reflect on the business implications of their decisions. In this way, AI can help create a continuous learning cycle: understand → investigate → execute → analyse → question → reflect.

    The integration of AI also provides an opportunity to make students more actively engaged with SAP by presenting managerial challenges like: A strategic customer requires urgent delivery, but the requested quantity cannot be fully confirmed. What could be causing the problem? What information would you investigate? What alternatives could the company consider? Students can use AI to generate hypotheses, investigate those hypotheses in SAP S/4HANA, use Copilot to analyse relevant data, and then defend their conclusions. The SAP system becomes the evidence base, while AI becomes a tool for exploration and reasoning.

    This approach also allows faculty to introduce AI-supported experiential learning into SAP courses. AI tool like ChatGPT can generate different customer and business scenarios, role-play customers or sales managers, create troubleshooting situations and challenge students with follow-up questions. Copilot can support data analysis, visualization and preparation of management-oriented reports using Order-to-Cash data. Students can consequently move from repetitive transaction execution to activities such as diagnosing process problems, comparing alternative decisions, interpreting data and communicating recommendations.

    The role of AI, therefore, is not simply to make SAP learning faster or easier. Its greater educational potential lies in shifting the focus from "Can the student execute the transaction correctly?" to broader questions such as "Does the student understand the business process?", "Can the student diagnose what is happening?", "Can the student use data and AI critically?", and "Can the student translate SAP information into a managerial decision?"

    Such an approach transforms O2C from a largely transaction-oriented practical exercise into a business simulation and decision-learning experience. Students still develop the essential hands-on SAP skills, but they also develop AI literacy, analytical thinking, problem-solving, business-process understanding and managerial judgment. The objective is not to have AI perform the student's SAP work; rather, it is to use AI to make the student more curious, more analytical and more engaged with the business problem that lies behind the transaction.

     

    Some Examples of AI Prompt for O2C Process

    • Act as an SAP business process consultant and ask AI tool to explain the Order-to-Cash process in SAP S/4HANA to an MBA student who understands basic sales and accounting but has never used SAP. Explain the business purpose of each major step and how information flows from one step to another.
    • Asking AI to explain how a sales order, delivery, goods issue, billing document and accounting document are related in an SAP S/4HANA Order-to-Cash process. Give a simple business example
    • Gave students a 3-page customer contract PDF. Ask them to use AI tool to extract SAP SD configuration requirements, create the customer master, and process the order in the live system within defined time frame. Write a summary of learnings.
    • Why can a sales order be created even when the requested quantity is not immediately available?
    • What is the business significance of the delivery block in an O2C process?
    • What could happen to customer satisfaction, inventory and revenue recognition if goods issue is delayed?
    • What happens to the customer's outstanding receivable?
    • A customer order for 500 units has been created, but only 300 units are confirmed for delivery. Identify possible business and SAP-related reasons and explain how a consultant should investigate the issue.
    • Generate five different Order-to-Cash business scenarios for an MBA SAP class. Each scenario should involve a different customer, product, quantity, delivery requirement and business problem. Ensure that the scenarios require students to analyze the implications for sales order, delivery, inventory and billing.
    • A customer has placed an order for 2,000 units. Only 1,200 units are available, the customer has a strict delivery deadline, and the sales manager wants to maximize customer satisfaction without creating excessive inventory pressure. Analyze the situation and recommend how the O2C process should be managed.

    AI can help in improving Learning Outcomes

    • On-Demand Clarification: Students stuck on why a process steps to be followed in a certain order can ask AI rather than waiting for the next class.
    • Active, Not Passive Learning: Instead of memorizing process sequences, students can use AI to build their own models from SAP export – reinforcing the “Why” behind each transaction.
    • Document-heavy Scenarios Made Traceable: Real Business scenarios involve contracts, RFQs, and invoices. AI allows students practice with realistic, messy documents rather than oversimplified examples.
    • Cross-function thinking: Students can use AI to get clear understanding of cross-functional integrated system process used by O-2-C of SAP.
    • Scenario Variation: Faculty can use AI tool to generate number of different scenarios with varied terms – giving every student a different case and reducing copy-paste submissions.
    • Error-Injection: Faculty can use AI to inject a deliberate errors into a dataset forcing students to identify and correct --- this helps in assessing diagnostic skills.

     Conclusion

    • The Order-to-Cash process provides an excellent environment for integrating generative AI into SAP education because it combines business processes, transactional data, cross-functional dependencies and managerial decisions.
    • AI tools like ChatGPT can serve as a conceptual tutor, questioning partner, scenario generator and troubleshooting companion, while Microsoft Copilot can add significant value when students work with Excel, PowerPoint, Word and other Microsoft 365-based learning activities and O2C datasets.
    • The ultimate objective, however, should not be to teach students to use AI to complete SAP assignments faster. It should be to teach them to combine AI, SAP and human judgment effectively.
    Explore further: Free, hands-on AI resources for teaching with SAP
    Extend the topic with free resources that bring AI into teaching through practical SAP scenarios:
    • Sales Processes in SAP S/4HANA Cloud: The Academic Lesson combines an end-to-end sales scenario with hands-on exposure to Joule, SAP’s AI assistant.
    • Tabular AI prediction: This faculty guide to SAP-RPT Playground introduces students to predictive AI using business data, without requiring coding.
    • Agentic AI: This faculty guide to building AI agents with Joule Studio explores agentic AI, where AI can plan, decide, and act. Faculty can use Joule Studio to introduce students to building AI agents in an enterprise context.
